[Public Projection](../records/jeffries_v_harleston_merits_1997-11-17.md#public-projection). Stone-Zsela's separate writing concurs in vacatur and Part II but would classify the address as citizen speech as a matter of law and categorically exclude offense, controversy, audience hostility, embarrassment, reputational pressure, and viewpoint-reaction disruption as sufficient grounds for punishment of this private public-concern speech. Title and subject matter do not convert the unaffiliated address into university speech. Assigned teaching, administration, and delegated chair speech remain controllable; independently proved nonperformance, threats, harassment, official discrimination, insubordination, misuse of authority, and other regulable misconduct remain lawful grounds. He requires proof of each defendant's substantial or motivating causal role and permits an independently lawful same-decision defense, but considers conflicting verdicts and distinct roles to require a limited new trial on those matters, immunity, and relief. He would neither reinstate inconsistent verdicts nor decide particular liability, immunity, damages, or precise prospective relief. His categorical substantive limit and compulsory-trial remedy lack a Court majority; his Part II join contributes to controlling law as identified above.

O'Connor, joined by Scalia and Thomas, would affirm on the employment balance. She gives weight to the unaffiliated public-concern setting and nonpolicymaking role, but finds that consequential administrative responsibilities and supported recruitment, fundraising, faculty, and community interests justify the chair-term action in light of the reasonable-expectation finding without waiting for actual harm. The dissent does not make sincere belief, offensive content, retained tenure, or the forecast automatically decisive, invent sponsorship or deficient performance, or adopt the nine-vote cause rationale or final immunity ruling as an alternative ground. Its balance and affirmance are noncontrolling.

### Rybar — November 24, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/united_states_v_rybar_merits_1997-11-24.md#public-projection). Stone-Zsela concurs in Parts I–II but dissents from Part III and would affirm Counts I and III through an independent arms application. Fully automatic repeated fire through one trigger function supplies the relevant characteristic; restricting additions to civilian stocks of these completed weapons directly addresses its distinctive sustained-fire risk. Registration traces arms, while licensing and records alone do not prevent stock expansion. He finds that preventive fit sufficient for this substantial burden in these transactions. Prior lawful stock is a transition limit, not proof of greater safety or an age-based exception. Government channels do not make military usefulness disqualifying or immune; available ordinary firearms describe scope but substitutes alone do not justify a protected-arm prohibition. His position relies on identified weapons, not invented casualty findings, creates no universal dangerous- or military-arms rule or equivalence to ordinary semiautomatics, and resolves no components or accessories. Dismissed transfer charges supply no alternative conviction ground. This application is noncontrolling; the Court leaves it for remand.

### Richenberg — December 8, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/richenberg_v_cohen_merits_1997-12-08.md#public-projection). Stevens, joined by Stone-Zsela, Souter, and Ginsburg, would reverse and set the discharge aside on an as-applied equality ground. The actual explanations inadequately connect ordinary attraction to likely prohibited conduct or explain rejection of the sworn undertaking and supporting evidence; receipt of rebuttal evidence is insufficient if the reasons deprive it of meaningful effect. Hypothetical lawful relationships and uncertainty about all future conduct do not supply the missing link. Military deference gives the Government's credibility reading weight but does not permit an appellate inference to replace the actual decision's required connection. The dissent preserves the policy and ordinary scrutiny, requires neither completed acts nor individual operational harm, and makes neither good service nor denial automatically dispositive. Lawful further military proceedings remain available without unconditional reinstatement, backpay, or resolution of every retention qualification. It adopts no independent APA, speech, or due-process ground.

Stone-Zsela's additional dissenting statement joins that equality ground and complete set-aside remedy, specifying that further military action must rest on a supported individualized finding of actual conduct, propensity, intent, or credibility under a lawful rule. Inability to predict every future relationship does not itself establish intent to violate military rules; additional explanation alone would not substitute for removing this discharge. Both dissenting positions are noncontrolling.

### Jefferson — December 9, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/jefferson_v_city_of_tarrant_jurisdictional_dismissal_1997-12-09.md#public-projection). Stevens would exercise jurisdiction under Ritchie's binding practical-finality holding notwithstanding his earlier dissent there. A merely possible later appeal does not answer whether repeated presentation of a settled federal issue serves any useful finality purpose. Alabama conclusively resolved the federal remedy issue and bound the trial court, which in his view permits review. This jurisdictional dissent decides no federal damages merits or final merits mandate and is noncontrolling.

### Hudson — December 10, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/hudson_v_united_states_merits_1997-12-10.md#public-projection). Stone-Zsela joins Parts I and III and affirmance on the combined actual-operation analysis under Ursery and Hendricks. The sanctions' accountability and protective functions differ from Kurth Ranch and Hendricks; he neither joins the independent Halper accounting ground nor rejects Halper's force. Different operations, excessiveness, and offense identity remain open. Scalia, joined by Thomas, would require successive criminal prosecutions and reject Halper's freestanding civil multiple-punishment method while permitting inquiry whether nominally civil proceedings are actually criminal. That theory lacks a majority and does not displace Halper.

### Joiner — December 15, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/general_electric_co_v_joiner_merits_1997-12-15.md#public-projection). Stevens joins Parts I–II but would vacate for the Eleventh Circuit to evaluate the actual cumulative method under the correct standard. Individually inconclusive studies do not necessarily defeat a combined inference, and the reported use of at least thirteen researchers and World Health Organization materials merits attention to the whole method. He commands neither admission nor a causation finding. Breyer joins the Court in full and suggests existing lawful assistance, including Rule 706 court-appointed experts and management of foundation inquiries, for difficult tentative science; no appointment, hearing, panel, or mandatory procedure follows. Stone-Zsela joins the uniform-review and inferential-fit rules and reversal, but not the particular PCB-only discretionary application, preserving the alternative exposure questions and remaining action. Their additional positions are noncontrolling.

### City of Chicago — December 15, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/city_of_chicago_v_international_college_of_surgeons_merits_1997-12-15.md#public-projection). Ginsburg, joined by Stevens, would affirm because general grants do not sufficiently transfer Illinois's assigned appellate task of closed-record agency review with presumptively correct facts. An independent federal-rights suit differs; common facts, a federal issue, and possible later abstention do not answer the antecedent power objection. Stone-Zsela joins Part I and reversal but would additionally direct the District Court to recognize jurisdiction and then decide retention, stay, or remand under §1367(c), abstention, and remedial law. His instruction neither commands retention nor finds abstention warranted and does not control the appellate mandate.

### Tanford — December 22, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/tanford_v_brand_merits_1997-12-22.md#public-projection). Scalia's dissenting Part I, joined by Kennedy and Thomas, would affirm because the brief traditional adult ceremony, genuine abstention, and absence of demonstrated unconstitutional pressure fall outside the existing secondary-school prohibitions. They acknowledge official devotional attribution. Thomas alone additionally joins Scalia's Part II historical-accommodation and compulsion account; Kennedy does not join that methodology. Kennedy's separate statement retains Lee's substantial practical pressure without requiring legal penalties, but finds none on this mature, optional, mobile audience's facts and declines to extend the independent sponsorship prohibition here. None of these positions changes the controlling sponsorship rule or creates a universal historical exemption.

### Clanton — December 29, 1997

[Public Projection](../records/clanton_v_cooper_merits_1997-12-29.md#public-projection). Stone-Zsela joins the legal/factual boundary and preserved deliberate-deception applications but would also affirm denial on the third surviving theory: use of a coerced manufactured confession against Clanton's own liberty concerns her due process, not borrowed interrogation rights. Falsity, coercion, materiality, and cause remain contestable; hearsay, absence of indictment, and charge timing create no independent liability. He also proposes a contextual defense with the justificatory burden on the official and no duplicative excuse for deliberate violations. Crawford-El did not adopt that change; it supplies no majority burden shift or procedure, and Harlow/Anderson remains governing law. His position makes neither denial of immunity nor assumed facts a liability finding or entitlement to trial.

### Valot — January 5, 1998

[Public Projection](../records/valot_v_southeast_local_school_district_board_of_education_merits_1998-01-05.md#public-projection). Stone-Zsela joins petition protection and the count-1 remand but would affirm every remaining disposition. His own formulation protects lawful, non-sham use of an established administrative-benefits process without public-concern content while retaining anti-fraud measures, eligibility contests, neutral filing rules, lawful prospective change, and independent employment grounds. He considers the specific Petition Clause source sufficient without separate substantive-due-process or equality relief and seeks adjudication of sole retaliatory causation, personal defenses, and remedy without inferring every defendant's liability. His broader formulation and different component remedies do not control.

O'Connor, joined by Scalia and Thomas, joins Part II but would affirm the federal defense judgment under the employee public-concern requirement. The applications sought personal income replacement; formality does not, for them, remove the employment dispute from that requirement. They rely neither solely on lack of renewal entitlement nor on a claim that successful petitioning cannot produce retaliation, presumed fraud, or a general fiscal license to punish independently protected conduct. Their petition and related-component positions are noncontrolling.

### Smith — January 12, 1998

[Public Projection](../records/smith_v_mattox_merits_1998-01-12.md#public-projection). Stone-Zsela joins Parts I–II and affirmance: the assumed absence of resistance, controlled position, and additional blow after complaint, rather than fracture alone, defeat the claimed legal immunity; earlier danger supplies no categorical authorization and disputed resistance cannot replace the assumed facts. He again proposes a contextual defense placing the justificatory burden on the official and rejecting a duplicative excuse for deliberate violations. The Court does not adopt that proposal, Crawford-El did not replace Harlow/Anderson, and the current objective defense remains intact. He preserves actual opportunities, reasonable mistakes, contrary supported facts, and remaining liability and remedial requirements. This proposed doctrinal change remains noncontrolling as in Clanton.

[Public Projection](../records/baker_v_general_motors_corp_merits_1998-01-13.md#public-projection). ### Chunk-5 published noncontrolling positions

#### Glendora v. Porzio, No. 97-7300. — 1998-03-09

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to action | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion and order of the Court, Part I | Per curiam | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Denies present financial leave | Particular-paper assessment and paid-compliance opportunity |
| Opinion and order of the Court, Part II | Per curiam | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Declines future restriction | Separate fit and inadequacy-of-individual-treatment ground |
| Dissent from Part I, joining Part II | Stevens | Stone-Zsela | Would grant present financial leave | Discretionary access for ordinary petition screening |

These published joins disclose no vote on the underlying certiorari petition.

**Stevens, joined by Stone-Zsela, dissenting from Part I and joining Part II.** The dissent would accept the present papers under the financial-leave rules for ordinary petition screening. The concrete service and hearing allegations warrant that discretionary course despite the serious independent obstacles. Alleged false service and judicial acceptance do not themselves establish state action by private counsel, conspiracy, or an available collateral challenge to the state judgment. Martin permits supported present denials but does not compel denial in every difficult case; the dissent's preferred exercise of discretion does not displace the Court's rule. Granting financial leave would neither excuse a jurisdictional defect nor revive the Second Circuit appeal, establish the allegations, grant certiorari, appoint counsel, or award relief. The dissent joins the separate refusal of prospective controls because present deficiencies and filing volume do not establish inadequacy of individual treatment.

#### Gray v. Maryland, No. 96-8653. — 1998-03-09

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Supports vacatur and remand | Direct-accusation redaction rule and application |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | O'Connor | Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Supports vacatur and remand | Preservation-qualified Chapman review and absence of an automatic retrial or acquittal |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | — | Vacate and remand; would direct determination of harmless error | Joins Part I; states immediate-context application and a distinct affirmative remand instruction |
| Dissent | Scalia | Kennedy and Thomas | Would affirm on the preserved redaction question | Richardson facial-versus-inferential line, limiting instruction and separate preservation of prosecutorial-use questions |

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment.** Stone-Zsela joins Part I. The blanks, grammar, limited named participants and prosecutor's immediate connection between Bell's information and Gray's arrest directly identify whose name was removed. The jury need not wait for later independent evidence to identify the accused, so an instruction cannot cure the uncross-examined accusation. His reliance on immediate context explains the preserved admission objection; it creates no separate ruling that the follow-up question itself was a preserved independent constitutional wrong. He would direct the state court to determine harmless error, without deciding it here, and permit consideration of materially different redactions or lawful trial-management alternatives. He does not join Part II's limitation of the remand instruction to a properly available harmless-error contention. Joint trials, genuinely neutral wording, independently admissible confessions and cross-examined testimony remain outside his prohibition.

**Scalia, joined by Kennedy and Thomas, dissenting.** The dissent would apply Richardson's distinction between a confession that identifies the accused on its face and one that becomes incriminating through inference from other evidence. Bell's statement contains two deletions, while other testimony describes six participants and only one other defendant is at this trial. A blank does not uniquely identify Gray without a further inference. Conspicuous editing alone is not the powerfully incriminating express accusation for which Bruton displaces the ordinary presumption that jurors follow limiting instructions. The dissent objects to a rule encouraging concealed edits or substantive rewriting, and would affirm on the preserved confession-admission issue. It does not treat instructions as a cure for every confrontation problem or eliminate Rule 14 severance and evidentiary protection beyond the constitutional minimum. The prosecutor's follow-up question presents a separate issue: the State says an arrest warrant preceded the confession and characterizes the question as a transition, and no contemporaneous objection to that question is identified. The dissent would not use it to circumvent preservation or to transform the preserved redaction question into a different adjudication.

#### Lewis v. United States, No. 96-7151. — 1998-03-09

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I: ACA inquiry and nonassimilation | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg | Six Justices adopt the governing framework and its application. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II: retained conviction and federal resentencing | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg | Eight Justices adopt the bounded conviction treatment and sentence-only remand. |
| Opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment | Scalia | Thomas | Both join Part II; they agree with Part I's judgment on a distinct generic-offense construction. |
| Dissent | Kennedy | No other Justice | Would allow assimilation and deny the requested federal resentencing. |

**Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, concurring in part and concurring in the judgment.** They read §13's act-or-omission language, informed by Williams, to refer to the generic criminal conduct. Federal law already punishes murder, so Louisiana cannot change its grade merely by adding a child-age element. They reject an open-ended inquiry into congressional policy as the method for determining assimilation and therefore do not join Part I. Their agreement on the judgment does not adopt its framework. They join Part II because the accepted federal conviction must receive lawful federal sentencing, with the departure question left to the sentencing court.

**Justice Kennedy, dissenting.** The ACA's federalism and local-conformity purpose supports a modified same-elements inquiry. Trivial wording and jurisdictional differences do not matter, but greater and lesser offenses can coexist for assimilation purposes. Williams prevents substitution where Congress selected a competing level of the same substantive element; federal murder law selected no competing victim-age threshold. Louisiana's child-age element therefore supplies a substantive distinction for him. He would allow assimilation and deny the requested federal resentencing because the assimilated offense supports its life punishment. His disagreement concerns that legal basis, not an independently asserted defect in the retained federal jury findings.

#### Quality King Distributors, Inc. v. L'anza Research International, Inc., No. 96-1470. — 1998-03-09

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Scalia | Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Rejects the categorical importation rule | Complete owner-or-authorized-person rule, statutory linkage and domestic-manufacture limit |
| Same opinion, partial join | Scalia | Stone-Zsela | Agrees with reversal | Lawful-owner reimportation proposition; no join in the authorized-person extension |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | Scalia | Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Reverses and returns for consistent further proceedings | No directed final judgment or new transaction findings |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Stone-Zsela | — | Agrees with reversal; would direct judgment for Quality King on the copyright-importation claim | Joins Part I only as to lawful-owner reimportation; rejects Part II's open remand in favor of the stated final relief |

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** Stone-Zsela joins Part I only insofar as it addresses copies made in the United States, sold abroad with the copyright owner's authorization and later reimported by their lawful owner. He does not join its broader rule for a person authorized by that owner. Section 602(a) invokes the §106(3) right, which §109(a) limits; crossing the border cannot recreate an exhausted distribution right, and territorial-pricing policy cannot do so either. He would direct entry of judgment for Quality King on the claim that this reimportation infringed that distribution right through §602(a), rather than leave that theory for further proceedings. Any preserved independent contract, trademark, labeling or consumer-protection claim remains governed by its own law. His disposition would not decide foreign manufacture, unauthorized reproductions, counterfeits, reproduction rights, trademark confusion or contractual duties enforceable against a contracting party.

#### Aktepe v. United States; Eleventh Circuit No. 96-2167. — 1998-03-10

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Kennedy | O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas and Breyer | Affirms | Complete claim-specific nonjusticiability ground and limits |
| Dissent | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, Souter and Ginsburg | Would vacate and remand | Issue-specific separation of execution allegations from policy choices; no guaranteed surviving claim |

**Stevens, joined by Stone-Zsela, Souter and Ginsburg, dissenting.** The dissent would vacate and remand for separate examination of the claims. The intended simulation and accidental live firing supply a concrete reason to distinguish execution from design; listing training and command purposes does not establish that every allegation requires choosing policy. Gilligan's reservation of specific-injury cases and Nixon's claim-specific limitation oppose the blanket effect of the judgment. Weiss and Loving preserve enforceable legal constraints despite military subject matter, and Dalton does not supply general executive insulation.

The dissent accepts that a court cannot invent a safer training rule, call it operational, and thereby evade the political-question doctrine. The remand would require the Eleventh Circuit to identify which allegations actually require selection of constitutionally committed military policy or lack manageable standards, without guaranteeing a surviving negligence claim, discovery, liability or compensation. No particular written protocol is found or presumed violated. Statutory coverage, sovereign immunity, Feres, causation, damages and the justiciability of any specifically identified high-level policy challenge remain unresolved. The dissent's proposed examination is not the Court's mandate.

#### Triestman v. United States; lower-court No. 96-2563, 124 F.3d 361; no Supreme Court docket number assigned. — 1998-03-12

| Writing | Author | Joins | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Per curiam | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | The statutory bar requires dismissal of this attempted ordinary review; independent collateral questions are not decided. |
| Concurrence | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Joins the Court's opinion and states a separate savings-clause view of what dismissal leaves open. |

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring.** He joins the jurisdictional dismissal and would give effect to both Congress's restrictions on repetitive litigation and the retained savings clause. In his view, an intervening interpretation that applies to the conviction and supports a substantial claim that the conduct was outside the criminal statute can permit §2241 consideration when no effective earlier §2255 opportunity existed. Inability to satisfy successive-motion criteria alone is insufficient. The prisoner must establish eligibility and entitlement to relief separately, and the Government retains its lawful defenses. Neither Article III nor a preference for review creates jurisdiction; Felker's distinct original route remains subject to its statutory and Rule 20 conditions. Complete foreclosure of meaningful review would raise a separate Suspension Clause question, which this disposition does not decide.

He regards the reported protective-storage plea account as presenting a substantial question under Bailey's active-employment rule that warrants a genuine opportunity to establish the asserted claim through an available savings-clause process. Intent, availability, possession and an officer's perception of danger do not substitute for active use. Failure of a use theory does not establish innocence of every alternative: carrying must be legally available and proved under its own elements, and aiding and abetting requires a substantive firearm offense and intentional assistance rather than presence or awareness. No finding establishes attempted firing, innocence, or savings-clause eligibility.

Triestman's earlier factual-basis objections and his supplemental Bailey submission must be acknowledged. They do not conclusively establish whether the earlier legal framework and procedures afforded an effective opportunity. The proper court may decide on an adequate existing record, obtain appropriate submissions or allow necessary factual development under governing law. An allegation does not satisfy every gateway or merits element, but eligibility does not require already prevailing on ultimate relief. No new burden, exhaustion requirement, unlimited retries, universal oral or evidentiary hearing, automatic release or favorable outcome follows. The plea's legal effect, available defenses and appropriate remedy require their own lawful determination; separate drug convictions are not resolved by the firearm question. These are his views of what dismissal leaves open, not holdings of the Court or relief ordered in this proceeding.

#### W.P. v. Verniero; Third Circuit No. 96-5416. — 1998-03-16

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Souter | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer | Rejects punishment relief | Common civil classification under both presented clauses |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | Souter | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Preserves advance review and State persuasion for tier and plan | Substantive state constraint, hearing and burden allocation |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III-A | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer | Affirms heightened proof for risk classification | Clear and convincing factual basis and tier determination |
| Opinion announcing the judgment, Part III-B | Souter | Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer | Affirms heightened proof for notification plan | Four-Justice plan-specific explanation; Stone-Zsela agrees only with this judgment component |
| Opinion of the Court, Part IV | Souter | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Leaves emergency issue unripe | No approval or categorical prohibition of exceptional notice procedure; Stone-Zsela agrees in disposition only |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | — | Affirms | Joins Parts I and III-A; separate ordinary-process safeguards; judgment-only agreement on Parts II and III-B; emergency disposition only |
| Dissent in part, joining Parts II, III-A, III-B and IV | Stevens | — | Would grant retrospective Ex Post Facto relief; otherwise joins the indicated process disposition | Punitive-operation objection; conditional process joins when civil notification remains available |
| Concurrence in part in the judgment and dissent in part | Scalia | Thomas in full; O'Connor and Kennedy on proof quantum only | Rejects punishment relief; would remove heightened proof while retaining State persuasion and advance review | Separate successive-criminal-prosecution ground and preponderance process ground; joins Parts II and IV |

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment.** Stone-Zsela joins the civil-classification and heightened risk-classification portions. Public protection and a civil structure do not remove the need for timely notice, disclosure of the basis, an opportunity to contest, a neutral decisionmaker, written reasons and clear and convincing State proof before the broad notification at issue. The State controls the evidence and proposes the classification; an erroneous high tier can irreversibly affect housing, work, safety and status. A prompt adversarial process can reduce error without defeating protection. His express affirmance includes retention of the notification-plan injunction, but he adopts no plan-specific explanation and does not join the separate state-entitlement analysis. On the unripe emergency component he agrees only with the disposition and adds no emergency ground. His stated safeguards supply no majority adoption of a new general written-reasons or disclosure code. Confidential registration and lower-tier treatment remain subject to their own law; every internet registry, lifetime classification without review and affirmatively punitive operation remain unresolved.

**Stevens, dissenting in part.** Stevens would reverse the denial of Ex Post Facto relief and require an injunction against retrospective Tier 2/3 notification for this defined class. The affirmative official broadcast of conviction and predicted dangerousness, its criminal-history trigger and enduring cumulative burdens resemble imposed shaming. Risk and audience limits deserve weight but do not alter that combined character on his assessment. Ursery's dissenting approach and the actual-operation holdings of Hendricks and Hudson support looking beyond the civil label. He does not attribute every private attack to the State or decide independent Double Jeopardy offense identity. Because the Court leaves civil notification available, he joins the indicated process portions, including clear and convincing proof for both tier and plan.

**Souter's Part III-B, joined by Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer.** These four would apply clear and convincing persuasion to the plan as well as the classification because unnecessary geographic or audience expansion causes the same irreversible disclosure. The State prepares the plan and its initial justification; factual disputes, atypical risks and the actual likely-encounter limit make stronger assurance useful without demanding certainty. Continuing registration and monitoring reduce the comparative cost of mistaken undernotification. This is the rationale of four Justices, not a controlling general plan-quantum rule.

**Scalia, joined by Thomas; O'Connor and Kennedy join the proof-quantum portion only.** Scalia and Thomas reject the Ex Post Facto challenge because the particular risk-tailored warning scheme is genuinely civil and protective on this record. They separately reject the Double Jeopardy challenge because that civil warning process is not a successive criminal prosecution. They preserve their Hudson disagreement with a freestanding Halper civil multiple-punishment method; that view does not overrule Halper. All four proof-quantum dissenters accept the substantive state interest, advance opportunity and State persuasion for both tier and plan, but would permit preponderance. Mathews also accounts for potential victims, the danger of underclassification and existing safeguards. Noncustodial tailored warnings do not impose Addington's physical custody or Santosky's family-status severance; neither serious consequences nor a protected interest mechanically requires heightened certainty. Sahhar's different commitment and discharge rules demonstrate the need to preserve the actual legal operation. Their proposed modification would remove only the heightened quantum, preserving the remainder of the ordinary-process injunction.

### Chunk-6 published noncontrolling positions

#### Almendarez-Torres v. United States — 1998-03-24

[Record](../records/almendarez_torres_v_united_states_merits_1998-03-24.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg | Statutory element classification, charging consequence and resentencing remedy |
| Opinion announcing the judgment, Part II | Scalia | Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg | Constitutional-avoidance explanation; no definitive constitutional classification rule |
| Concurrence in Part I and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Definitive constitutional ground for the element classification; does not join Part II's reservation of that question |
| Dissent | O'Connor | Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer | Penalty construction and bounded constitutional permission for this recidivist enhancement; would affirm |

**Scalia, joined by Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg, Part II.** These Justices regard the tenfold increase in maximum punishment as presenting serious doubt about Congress's ability to assign the aggravating fact solely to a sentencing judge. The element reading is fairly available, so they apply constitutional avoidance and decline to decide that ultimate question. McMillan's unchanged ceiling and Watts's ordinary sentencing setting do not eliminate the doubt. The risk of prejudice from prior-conviction evidence can be addressed through adequate admissions or other proper proof rather than removal of an element from the charge.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in Part I and in the judgment.** The constitutional allocation turns on the fact's legal effect. A fact necessary to increase the authorized maximum from two years to twenty years performs the work of an element and must be charged and either validly admitted as an element of that offense or proved to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt. Legislative placement cannot transfer that work entirely to the sentencing judge. Gaudin protects element determination; Watts permits ordinary judicial sentencing findings only within conviction-based authority. Custis concerns collateral attack, and Old Chief demonstrates how adequate status proof can avoid unnecessary prejudice. The admitted facts here do not cure an indictment that never charged the aggravated offense. This position permits consideration of prior convictions within a separately authorized range, preserves Custis's collateral-review limits, requires no prejudicial details when adequate admission or stipulation establishes the element, and decides no sentencing fact that leaves the statutory maximum unchanged.

**O'Connor, joined by Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer, dissenting.** Subsection (b)(2)'s recidivist subject, reciprocal cross-references and punishment structure make it a penalty provision for the alien already described in subsection (a). Existing conviction status differs from facts about commission of the present crime, and Congress may treat that prior adjudication as a sentencing factor in this setting. The admission supports the application but is not a substitute for their statutory classification. These Justices acknowledge that McMillan and Watts do not alone resolve an increased ceiling; the distinct recidivism ground does that work. They would affirm without adopting unlimited legislative power to remove offense elements or resolving an unpresented subsidiary proof-burden question.

| Opinion of the Court, Part III-A | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | The offered voluntary interview does not establish compelled self-incrimination |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III-B | O'Connor | Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | The conclusion also survives an assumed ordinary civil adverse inference, with actual-compulsion and automatic-penalty limits; Stone-Zsela does not join this additional ground |

**Kennedy, joined by Scalia and Thomas, concurring in part and in the judgment.** Ohio's procedure does not constrain the ultimate mercy decision, and the appellate analogy supplies no right to the process requested. Dumschat and the substantive distinction applied in Sandin and Johnson resolve these pleaded process claims. These Justices do not join the affirmative retained-life framework or its application; their judgment agreement adds no join to Part II. They preserve independently grounded constitutional prohibitions and fully join the self-incrimination analysis, including its actual-compulsion and automatic-penalty limits.

**Stevens, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** A prisoner remains alive, and an established procedure integral to the State's final decision to take life must afford basic fairness and meaningful participation. His Dumschat position and Evitts's established-process principle support bounded inquiry into the process as a whole, even though clemency need not replicate a trial and no right to mercy exists. He joins the minimum safeguard but would preserve the due-process remand to consider the relevant materials rather than hold these pleadings insufficient. He finds no violation already established and prescribes none of the requested safeguards automatically. He joins both self-incrimination grounds, distinguishing this voluntary invitation from a command backed by a serious threatened sanction.

#### United States v. Scheffer — 1998-03-31

[Record](../records/united_states_v_scheffer_merits_1998-03-31.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Thomas | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Reliability-based constitutional permission, its application and limits, reversal and bounded remand |
| Concurrence | Scalia | Souter and Thomas | Joins the Court and adds the category-specific credibility-role and collateral-litigation justifications |
| Concurrence | Kennedy | O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer | Joins the Court; distinguishes constitutional permission from evidentiary policy and declines the two additional justifications |
| Dissent | Stevens | No other Justice | Would affirm removal of the categorical obstacle and permit lawful foundation consideration, without commanding admission |

**Scalia, joined by Souter and Thomas, concurring.** In addition to reliability, two features independently justify this category-specific rule: preserving the court members' responsibility to judge credibility against a scientific certification of the accused's truthfulness, and avoiding recurring collateral litigation over examiner qualifications, question design, countermeasures and interpretation. These grounds permit this polygraph rule; they do not reject every expert opinion bearing on credibility or every defense proffer requiring time. All three fully join the Court's reliability ground. Their additional grounds have three votes and are not controlling.

**Kennedy, joined by O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer, concurring.** Reasonable disagreement about polygraph reliability permits the present rule, but constitutional permission does not establish that a categorical ban is the best evidentiary policy. These Justices decline to make protection of the factfinder from ultimate-issue assistance or collateral-litigation concerns independently sufficient grounds here. Their qualification preserves the possible significance of a stronger future proffer without finding this one admissible, requiring a new hearing or altering the present judgment.

**Stevens, dissenting.** A total prohibition prevents an accused from showing that an important defense proffer has a sufficient foundation. The Government administered this examination, and its results bear on the credibility of the denial of knowing ingestion. Egelhoff's meaningful opportunity to rebut the actual element and Rock's treatment of unsupported categorical exclusion favor lawful foundation review. Allowing Scheffer to speak does not by itself answer the exclusion of corroborative support. Stevens would sustain removal of the per se obstacle without deciding ultimate admission, acquittal or entitlement to a new trial before that inquiry. He preserves a concern under Article 36(a), which directs general federal criminal evidence principles so far as the President considers practicable and bars inconsistency with the military code, but does not rest his disposition on that unbriefed statutory question.

#### In re Dorsainvil; Third Circuit No. 96-8074, 119 F.3d 245. No separate Supreme Court docket is supplied — 1998-04-02

[Record](../records/in_re_dorsainvil_jurisdictional_dismissal_1998-04-02.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Per curiam | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Entire jurisdictional holding and dismissal |
| Concurrence | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Joins the Court; separate noncontrolling view of independent savings-clause consideration |

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring.** He joins the Court's dismissal and states his view of the independent process left open. Congress's restrictions on repetitive litigation and its retained savings clause must both have practical effect. An intervening interpretation that applies to the conviction and supports a substantial claim of noncriminal conduct may permit §2241 consideration when no effective earlier §2255 opportunity existed. Failure to satisfy the successive-motion criteria alone is insufficient. The prisoner must establish eligibility and entitlement to relief separately, and the Government retains its lawful defenses. Neither Article III nor the gravity of detention creates a new forum. Complete foreclosure of meaningful review would raise a distinct Suspension Clause question that this dismissal does not decide.

In his view, the first §2255 proceedings' completion before Bailey and the described firearm account present a substantial question for an actually available savings-clause process. Intent, protective storage, availability and possession do not replace active use. The reported reaching movements establish neither firing nor attempted firing; an officer's perception of danger is not the offense element. Failure of a use theory does not establish innocence of carrying or another legally available ground. The Government must establish that ground's elements and legal availability, and the court must examine the evidence and charge rather than treat the inclusion of carrying language as a complete verdict or harmlessness analysis.

An appropriate court may decide on an adequate existing record, receive appropriate submissions or permit necessary factual development under governing law. An allegation alone does not establish the required predicates, but access does not require already prevailing on ultimate relief. No new burden, exhaustion requirement, unrestricted retries, universal oral or evidentiary hearing, automatic release or favorable outcome follows. These are his noncontrolling views of what remains open, not an eligibility finding or a remand ordered by this Court.

#### United States v. Hinds — 1998-04-06

[Record](../records/united_states_v_hinds_merits_1998-04-06.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stevens | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Vacates the Fourth Circuit's affirmance and remands | Part I's complete property-function construction and application; Part II's existing-record mandate and constitutional nonreach |
| Same opinion, partial joins | Stevens | Stone-Zsela | Agrees that the affirmance cannot stand; opposes the Court's operative remand | Part I only as to independent work for the property-use element, insufficiency of owner relationships by themselves, and absence of a religious exemption; Part II only as to the independent Burks rule that evidentiary insufficiency requires acquittal and bars retrial to repair proof |
| Concurrence in part and dissent from the judgment and remand | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Would reverse and direct vacatur of the §844(i) conviction and entry of acquittal on that count | Active-commercial-use construction; present insufficiency and immediate acquittal; separate Agostini-based reason for rejecting the Establishment objection as a construction aid or alternative ground |

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting from the judgment and remand.** The enacted use requirement demands active employment of the building itself in commercial activity. The congregation's purchases, utilities, insurance, staff, donations, mail and national affiliation are economic relationships; they do not transform premises devoted to worship into property actively employed in commerce. The national denomination's annual redistribution of funds to missionaries, seminaries, institutions of higher education and other programs is the Government's strongest argument, but it still describes what the congregation paid and gave in support of worship, rather than commercial use of this building. Russell's rented premises illustrate the distinction because the property itself operated in the rental market. The Fourth Circuit stated the use element but answered it through the congregation's economic connections. Stone-Zsela considers the Government's proof insufficient now. Under Burks and Jacobson he would reverse, direct vacatur of the conviction and entry of acquittal, and deny another trial to repair that proof.

Lopez supplies avoidance context, not a constitutional judgment. Its connection-before-magnitude sequence raises doubt about a reading that reaches every building through an owner's insurance, purchases, payroll or gifts and their downstream economic consequences. Avoidance is available because Congress enacted a use limitation to construe; it permits no inserted element. The existence of jurisdictional wording is not itself a constitutional safe harbor. Lopez preserves genuine economic-class analysis under Wickard and Perez and does not require a substantial effect from each individual act. Stone-Zsela leaves Hinds's particular substantial-effect contention and the outer Commerce question undecided. Hale, Rybar and Kirk's protection of a valid machinegun regime does not dispense with this statute's different property-use element. Robinson's direct interference with operating business assets likewise supplies no all-purchases rule. Robertson's commercial enterprise transactions and Allied-Bruce's broader transaction-involving-commerce language do not replace §844(i)'s property-use text.

This is no religious exemption. Stone-Zsela reserves the reach of the statute over religious property itself used for a commercial enterprise, rental activity, substantial commercial leasing or materially mixed commercial use. He decides no particular application within those categories, no authority under another federal statute, including FACE's unchallenged worship branches, and no reach of differently worded statutes such as the Hobbs Act. Ordinary state arson law and independently valid federal charges retain their own elements and limits.

He separately rejects the Establishment objection as a reason to construe the statute differently for religious property or as an alternative ground for reversal. Under Lemon as Agostini modified it, a specific prohibition or distinct doctrine resolves conduct it covers; an established permissible relationship defeats a covered claim; otherwise a legally sufficient unresolved claim proceeds through attribution and function. Purpose, effects and entanglement are evidence within that inquiry, not independent or fallback prongs. The governmental act here is prosecution of an alleged arsonist, and its function is ordinary property protection. Everson's established relationship of general public-welfare services, including ordinary police and fire protection, resolves the objection, provided the criminal statute validly applies.

The prosecution organizes no worship, prescribes no religious profession or observance, adopts no doctrine, solicits no religious adherence, governs no theology, confers no religiously allocated civil authority and finances no devotion. Examining a congregation's operations to determine an offense element is not regulation of its religious teaching or governance. Tanford involved the government's own organized commencement worship and therefore a different function. Facial neutrality and the beneficiary's identity are contextual evidence, not independently decisive grounds. Stone-Zsela reaches neither the residual route nor an accommodation, funding, legislative-prayer or ceremonial question; free exercise and religious autonomy retain their distinct sources and burdens. His answer creates no rule permitting every governmental benefit to religion, supplies neither statutory coverage nor an enumerated power, and does not ground his reversal. The second granted question remains unreached; insofar as the Establishment objection falls outside the grant, this discussion states only his reason for declining to rely on it. No other Justice joins this separate explanation.

No complete A-771 opinion commands a majority. The limited interim proposition identified in Holding IV is independently supported by Kennedy, O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas and by Stone-Zsela's separate explanation. That express agreement supplies five votes for that proposition, without treating Stone-Zsela as joining Part III's additional analysis or combining incompatible rationales under Marks.

**Kennedy, joined by O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas, Part III's additional grounds.** These Justices separately distinguish international bindingness, domestic operation without further implementation, enforcement by these applicants against these officers, and the requested remedy. Even assuming bindingness, the present domestic-enforcement showing is insufficient. Article 94(2)'s permissive Security Council route is not declared exclusive. Blessing prevents an official title or §1983 label from automatically establishing a personal right; a distinct officer-equity theory still needs its own current federal duty. Neither comity nor §1651 creates one. They reject a blanket political-question ground and do not infer nonparty status, privity or failure to file.

They acknowledge Shipp and United Mine Workers preservation authority but find no necessary additional jurisdictional interval here. Under Atlantic Coast Line, grave injury and loss of requested relief do not themselves establish serious impairment of the Court's authority. An ungranted original complaint differs from Shipp's habeas appeal and Mine Workers's otherwise properly presented civil parties. Even if a proper statutory route were available, these Justices find a present interim denial possible without protection. They do not categorically reject Hale or Mitchum, settle the claimant's personal §1983 right, or announce that every international measure lacks domestic effect. These additional grounds have four joins, not the Court's majority.

**Stone-Zsela, signed explanation concurring in the denials.** He denies A-738 and A-771 because the described submissions do not sufficiently establish the domestic right, ongoing duty, jurisdiction and remedy supporting Paraguay's own requested protection through the respective review and original proceedings. An imminent consequence of a past notice failure does not, without the required legal connection, establish every predicate for relief against the officials. The Seminole holding preserves its particular officer route and leaves direct-State amenability without a controlling rationale; it is no categorical bar and supplies no treaty cause. He reserves the separate cause-of-action and original-jurisdiction questions, categorical treaty enforceability and ultimate prejudice.

For A-767 he independently applies Felker's retained original route, without requiring circuit authorization or importing the authorization-review bar. He finds no sufficient exceptional-original-relief showing or separately identified unfinished legally required process to justify the requested stay. The ICJ provisional request is serious international context, not itself the required domestic order. A treaty claim and execution's severity warrant consideration through an available procedure but do not themselves create a cause, exception or remedial power. His denials decide no accompanying petition or leave motion and neither order execution nor grant release. This writing is his Circuit Justice explanation for A-738 and his own statement on each original application. He adopts no additional §2283 necessity ground or colleague's complete opinion.

**Scalia, concurring.** He joins Kennedy's complete explanation and adds his Ohio Citizens distinction between suspending enforcement of a judgment and granting affirmative intervention withheld below. For A-738 and A-771 he would require a particularly clear legal entitlement for such extraordinary injunctions; the disputed present duty and domestic enforcement chain fail that showing. A-738 expressly requests an injunction, so the absence of a request in Ohio Citizens is not imported. Each denial also rests independently on the shared, more favorable interim inquiry. His additional formulation is not a general full-Court injunction rule adopted by the Court and supplies no ground for A-767.

**Stevens, joined by Ginsburg and Breyer, dissenting from denial of A-767.** They would use §2251's discretionary authority to stay execution only until 5 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time on April 16, or an earlier Court order, while the actual original petition and application receive consideration. The new international measure and serious domestic custody/channel question warrant that brief interval before the requested protection becomes impossible. Felker separates jurisdiction from entitlement; their proposal finds no original-writ entitlement and neither satisfies nor defeats an unverified Rule 20 condition. They order no response or hearing and invoke no automatic Lonchar command. Barefoot and Doran remain analogies, not replacements for the original channel. The remainder, including protection through disposition of the original petition, remains reserved; no ICJ-duration stay is proposed.

**Stevens, joined by Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, dissenting from denial of A-771.** They would enjoin the connected Virginia officials from executing Breard only until the same April 16 endpoint or earlier order, with earlier vacation required upon determination of the relevant want of jurisdiction or injunctive power. They identify a substantial question about whether the official-capacity consular claim fits Article III and §1251(b)(1), and whether Young permits prospective relief for the newly asserted April 9 duty against these officers rather than an impermissible State action under Monaco. Current Seminole and Coeur d'Alene make that inquiry substantial without answering it. The April 13 complaint and April 14 execution require, in their assessment, this brief period to determine the Court's own power.

They apply Shipp and United Mine Workers through §1651 and, assuming §2283 applies, expressly find its necessary-in-aid exception satisfied: execution would destroy the particular pre-execution protection whose jurisdictional availability the actual original action presents. They accept that uncertain merits and loss of requested relief ordinarily do not establish that necessity. Their conclusion is confined to this new substantial original-power inquiry and the defined necessary interval. They assume neither stranger status under Hale nor a successful §1983 right under Mitchum, attach no consul's exception to Paraguay, and invoke neither the federal-government exemption nor an existing domestic judgment. The administrative label creates no exception. Leave, longer relief, bindingness, domestic effect, cause and remedy remain undecided. No immunity waiver, mandatory new paper or hearing follows.

Each participating Justice's signed adoption or separate statement is specified below. The Chief Justice's explanation arises from the Fourth Circuit allotment; its majority-joined portions are the Court's opinion, not a separate concurrence.

**Justice Souter, concurring in the denial and joining Parts I and III.** Even assuming reviewability of the treaty's full-effect/default question, he finds no sufficient showing that correction of default would overcome the inadequately supported causal connection between omitted consular advice and the conviction or sentence. The noncapital offer, counsel's recommendation, Breard's refusal and the proposed different influence of consular assistance leave that independent remedial obstacle unresolved. He does not finally find absence of prejudice or adopt every default proposition in Part II. He adopts Part III's separate insufficiency assessment of the process claim and does not treat it as defaulted.

**Justice Stevens, dissenting; Ginsburg and Breyer join Part I of his dissent.** The three Justices would stay execution until disposition of petition No. 97-8214 unless modified or dissolved sooner; protection afterward would require further order. Article 36(2)'s full-effect condition presents a substantial question when the alleged failure to advise prevented timely invocation of the consular right. They find a reasonable probability of review and a significant possibility that correction of the lower court's treatment could require consequential further consideration. They recognize domestic procedural rules, the availability of the treaty text, the disputed causal effect and the need for a lawful remedy. They do not find novelty alone sufficient cause, final enforceability or prejudice proved, or a right to a writ. Their ground is the actual stay standard, not an automatic first-petition pause or a required hearing inferred from difficulty.

**Justice Stevens, Part II of his dissent, joined by no other Justice.** The separately preserved federal method claim also warrants protection in his view. Hicks and Evitts distinguish meaningful judicial adjudication of a protected sentencing interest from a demand for a favorable discretionary benefit. A substantially skewed pool could frustrate that protection, and a possible failure to address the actual theory creates sufficient prospects of a legally consequential correction. He acknowledges subsection (E)'s permission to choose the period of accumulation, the reported inclusion of life sentences, the untested comparability of the numerical allegations and independent collateral limits. He neither requires collection of every prosecution nor finds arbitrary review proved. His Woodard dissent's concern for an established process protecting life supports a bounded inquiry; the later Woodard decision does not itself supply prefinality law. Ginsburg and Breyer withhold assent to this independent process-sufficiency conclusion and join the Court's Part III instead.

**Signed adoptions.** O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas each deny the application and adopt the Chief Justice's Parts I–III in full as their signed reasons. Souter denies and adopts Parts I and III together with his own concurrence. Stevens would grant on his dissent's two grounds and adopts the Court's Part I standard. Ginsburg and Breyer each would grant on Part I of Stevens's dissent, adopt the Court's Parts I and III, and do not adopt Stevens's Part II. The Chief Justice's own signed explanation supplies his denial reasons and his Circuit Justice explanation.

#### Carriger v. Stewart; Ninth Circuit No. 95-99025 — 1998-04-16

| Opinion of the Court, Part II: gateway and state-finding correction | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Five require renewed correct analysis; no finding that the gateway now succeeds or fails |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III: distinct Brady elements and conditional full-file materiality | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Six support the conditional merits instruction; it establishes neither suppression nor gateway passage |

| Concurrence | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Joins Parts II–IV and the complete remand; explains why he would have affirmed outright under a bounded extension of Kyles |

Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas join no portion of the lead opinion. They reserve the pending-capital temporal question and do not reach a materiality disposition. Their join in O'Connor's dissent adopts neither her Part I join nor her Part III conditional materiality conclusion. No separate opinion is issued by any of those three Justices.

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring.** He joins the operative vacatur and complete remand, including Parts II–IV, while explaining why he would have affirmed the new-trial relief outright. He separates the Schlup gateway, a freestanding innocence claim, and the constitutional suppression claim. In his assessment, the new evidence permits gateway review, and the combined withheld impeachment undermines confidence in the conviction under Kyles. He does not accept a recanting witness's confession mechanically: incentives, consistency, physical corroboration and later repudiation matter, as does the original prosecution's dependence on the same witness's credibility. His agreement to require correct further analysis does not withdraw that personal assessment or convert it into the Court's finding.

He would extend Kyles's duty to learn to impeachment information about the State's own key witness in the State Department of Corrections' records when the prosecution relies on that witness and the records are readily accessible to the State. On that bounded theory, failure to obtain and disclose material favorable information is suppression even if the trial prosecutor never personally held the file. He would affirm conditional new-trial relief, permitting a lawful retrial, rather than declare innocence or order acquittal. His proposal does not impute every government office's knowledge or impose open-file or unrestricted investigative duties. The Court preserves this theory for lawful consideration but does not adopt it.

**Justice O'Connor, concurring in Parts I and III and dissenting from Parts II and IV; Justices Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas join the dissent only.** The four agree that the present writ instruction must be removed but would hold this submission insufficient under the controlling Schlup probability rule. Dunbar's possible guilt does not exclude Carriger's joint participation. The adverse family accounts, disputed but probative tape evidence, and supported state credibility finding retain force even when the confession and new impeachment are considered. In their view, those features make another gateway determination unnecessary: correcting the lower court's formulation still leaves the demanding probability showing unmet. They would preserve independently available unaddressed claims while foreclosing this otherwise-abusive Brady route on the present submission.

Their position neither reinstates a stricter gateway burden nor categorically excludes recantation, prisoner testimony, impeachment or trial-inadmissible evidence. They do not treat the state finding as conclusive on later evidence. O'Connor separately accepts Part I's bounded statutory construction and Part III's conditional full-file materiality; Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas reserve transition and do not reach materiality. All four reserve the acquisition duty rather than reject its constitutional merits, and find no established absence of actual case-team knowledge. Their reservation leaves any genuinely independent lawful future route to its own conditions.

#### Women’s Medical Professional Corp. v. Voinovich; Sixth Circuit Nos. 96-3157 and 96-3159.

[Record](../records/womens_medical_professional_corp_v_voinovich_merits_1998-04-20.md#public-projection)

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part; no joins.** Stone joins the complete Casey/Fargo standard and the required protection for grave, medically established danger of severe, lasting and potentially irreversible mental or emotional injury. He rejects both Salerno’s independent barrier and an independent numerical facial threshold. He would affirm invalidity of the D&X prohibition and deficient penal medical exceptions now. In his application, the definition reaches the predominant D&E method, and courts cannot cure that reach by rewriting the definition. Intentional performance supplies no adequate culpability concerning an erroneous clinical-necessity determination; an affirmative defense does not cure the initial criminal and civil exposure. He therefore opposes the categorical-notice vacatur and the Court’s decision to leave method invalidity for further substantive application. His application does not command the Court.

Stone leaves severability and precise relief to the lower court without reopening his invalidity holdings. Ohio may regulate a genuinely distinct procedure, prohibit postviability abortion outside necessary life-and-health circumstances, punish bad-faith or sufficiently culpable violations, and enforce evidence-based safety rules. His health protection excludes transient distress and unsupported assertion and creates no unrestricted physician veto. His agreement that relief belongs below does not join the Court’s particular saving-construction analysis or its interim-only treatment of unresolved method applications.

**Justice Kennedy, concurring in part and dissenting in part; no joins.** Kennedy joins the actual-wording notice holding, serious necessary mental-health protection, its lawful protective-construction inquiry and ordinary Ohio severability principles. His retained Casey protected-choice baseline and Fargo separate position distinguish the substantive adequacy of care from the intelligibility of a rule. A method-specific health defense cannot cure a separate prohibition that excludes necessary mental-health care.

He would reverse the previability method injunction under his reasonable-regulation approach. The act-defined restriction, actual alternative procedures and enacted health defense defeat this categorical challenge absent an established denial of protected choice or necessary care. He rejects the general residual lesser-burden substantiation rule and therefore does not join the six-step method remand or continued unresolved-method protection under that mandate. He neither requires failure in every application nor finds every alternative equally safe. Supported necessary-care applications remain protected; he does not approve the entire Act. His narrower regulatory approach supplies no substitute for the Court’s controlling framework.

**Justice Scalia, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Justice Thomas.** Scalia and Thomas join the bounded notice/fault holding and ordinary Ohio severability principles. Their Fargo position supports attention to the purposeful act and specified professional criteria, without a universal scienter cure, a bad-faith-only safe harbor or invented criminal and civil elements.

They would reverse the constitutional injunction under their continuing objection to Casey’s heightened abortion framework and their ordinary reasonable-regulation approach. They dissent from the required constitutional mental-health protection as well as the method remand. They acknowledge that Casey’s actual necessary-care rule is the controlling premise from which they dissent; they do not redescribe it as merely Doe’s statutory construction or a numerical test. Their position neither supplies a different statutory fact nor establishes professional immunity. Agreement on notice and severability adds no vote to their proposed reversal or to the Court’s health and method-remand rationales.
