#### Campbell v. Louisiana, No. 96-1584.

[Record](../records/campbell_v_louisiana_threshold_1998-04-21.md#public-projection)

Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, joins the personal-standing, selection-method, preservation and remand portions but dissents from third-party standing. They reject reliance on perceived institutional unfairness as the required injury and distinguish a defendant's interest in overturning his conviction from an excluded citizen's interest in jury service. Even accepting Powers, they regard selection of a single grand-jury foreperson outside defendant-conducted voir dire as lacking the relationship and visible exclusion on which that decision relied. Prospective jurors alleging systemic exclusion may seek declaratory or injunctive relief, and ordinary litigation expense does not, in their view, establish the necessary impediment. The intervening petit-jury conviction reinforces their objection to using another person's right to upset the conviction and their doubts about eventual due-process success. They nevertheless recognize standing to assert Campbell's own right. Their writing decides neither the personal claim's merits nor harmless error, and their continued criticism does not overrule Powers.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela joins the personal-standing ground and bounded remand. Campbell was subjected to the charging authority of the allegedly race-composed body, and lawful correction can address that personal injury. The direct route fully resolves the standing judgment, so he does not reach whether Campbell also may assert excluded jurors' rights. He likewise reserves the substantive due-process rule, discrimination merits and any eventual remedy; his nonreach does not join the separate writing's rejection of third-party standing.

#### California v. Deep Sea Research, Inc., No. 96-1400.

[Record](../records/california_v_deep_sea_research_inc_merits_1998-04-22.md#public-projection)

Justice Stevens joins the Court and supplies a broader historical admiralty explanation. His earlier Treasure Salvors reasoning assumed that officer-possession limits under Tindal and United States v. Lee also prevented a binding adjudication of the State's maritime title. He now regards the distinctive early admiralty understanding described by Justices Story and Washington as undermining that assumption: adjudication of the res can bind competing interests. Ordinary ejectment and officer litigation therefore do not automatically supply the limits of in-rem admiralty. He finds that broader account persuasive, while the Court decides only the unpossessed wreck. His explanation does not establish a controlling rule for State-possessed property or change the separate officer remedy in Coeur d'Alene.

Justice Kennedy, joined by Justices Ginsburg and Breyer, also joins the Court fully. They do not read its treatment of Treasure Salvors as permanently fixing possession versus nonpossession as the complete constitutional boundary. Historical doubts and Justice Stevens's maritime explanation leave that broader question open to reconsideration. Their reservation leaves intact both today's sufficient nonpossession rule and the binding adjudication it permits; it neither decides a State-possessed case nor supplies another majority holding.

#### Miller v. Albright, No. 96-1060.

[Record](../records/miller_v_albright_merits_1998-04-22.md#public-projection)

### Stevens's opinion announcing the judgment

Justice Stevens would sustain the recognition requirement even under demanding intermediate scrutiny. Reliable parentage identification and an opportunity for a relationship with the citizen parent and this country during childhood are important objectives. Birth ordinarily establishes maternity and an initial opportunity for connection in a way conception alone does not establish paternity or knowledge of the child's existence. Lehr permits attention to a timely legal step rather than biology alone. The amended alternatives include acknowledgment and adjudication, not only marriage or the father's voluntary assent; the available former route likewise required legitimation before twenty-one. Neither deadline was met.

He regards the distinction as substantially fitted to those objectives, rather than justified by assumed paternal irresponsibility. Virginia, Kelley and Klinger allow relevant differences without requiring the least restrictive means. Accepted biology and later reliable proof do not supply the childhood recognition Congress selected. The deadline concerns the qualifying act's occurrence, not a prohibition on later proving an act that was timely. He neither assumes every mother creates enduring American ties nor upholds every father-only condition. He does not decide Fiallo's maximum deference or deny all constitutional remedial power.

### O'Connor's concurrence, joined by Kennedy

These Justices recognize Miller's concrete injury but regard the heightened sex-equality claim as her father's. Powers, Singleton and Campbell require a sufficiently close relationship and a genuine impediment in addition to injury. The father brought his own claim and did not appeal dismissal; ordinary expense, inconvenience and transfer do not establish the obstacle they require. Craig and the excluded-juror cases do not, in their view, eliminate that requirement.

Assuming consideration of Miller's own objection, they treat its classification as parentage rather than her own sex and apply rational review. Recognition during minority reasonably connects the citizenship route with the citizen parent. A separate legitimacy-versus-illegitimacy challenge falls outside the granted comparison. They do not join Stevens's heightened-scrutiny result. Under heightened scrutiny they would reject the stereotyped justification, but their standing conclusion prevents that assessment from becoming their operative adjudication of the father's claim. They also do not join Scalia's citizenship-remedy rule or establish general immunity of nationality legislation from review.

### Scalia's concurrence, joined by Thomas

These Justices accept Miller's permission to assert her father's claim under existing Craig precedent, notwithstanding their earlier misgivings about third-party standing. They consider her the appropriate affected challenger and decline O'Connor's demanded degree of hindrance. Their disagreement concerns the requested remedy.

Wong Kim Ark and Bellei distinguish Fourteenth Amendment birthright from foreign-birth citizenship governed by Congress's enactments. Pangilinan forbids conferring citizenship contrary to statutory conditions. Sections 1401 and 1409 form an integrated grant: the latter's unmet condition is not a later confiscation of citizenship already conferred unconditionally by the former. In their view, Congress's naturalization power and §1421(d)'s prescribed manner and conditions prevent judicial enlargement of that grant; that specific limit defeats reliance on the INA's general §406 severability clause. Mathews permits either extension or withdrawal to cure unequal treatment and does not make extension inevitable. Interlocking paternal and maternal conditions prevent assuming Congress would select the particular enlargement requested, and Westcott's ordinary benefit remedy does not resolve the citizenship-specific issue.

Their ground remains legal after accepting paternal citizenship, sufficient presence, undisputed biology and the former route's lack of a support promise. They do not decide the sex classification, the Government's separate extraterritorial own-right objection, withdrawal of anyone else's citizenship or a universal bar to constitutional review.

### Ginsburg's dissent, joined by Souter and Breyer

These Justices regard Miller herself as denied a statutory opportunity according to her citizen parent's sex. That classification does not cease to be sex-based because the child may be female or male. Virginia, Kelley and Klinger require scrutiny of the actual distinction and its substantial fit. Independently, Craig and Powers permit assertion of the father's right: the Government obtained his dismissal and transfer while the daughter's identical controversy continued, and the resulting practical obstacles suffice under their assessment. They do not claim that an appeal was legally impossible. Calling Miller an alien assumes the answer to her claim of citizenship at birth; Fiallo's admission preferences for conceded aliens do not settle that claim.

Reliable biological proof is important and can justify suitable evidence requirements reflecting actual differences between maternity and paternity. It does not justify the additional categorical age restriction here. Later reliable evidence can establish parentage, while a timely formal act does not itself ensure durable family or national ties. The maternal route requires no continuing custody, support or transmission of American culture. Actual knowledge, care and connection can be examined without sex as an overbroad substitute. This is a substantial-fit objection, not a least-restrictive-means requirement or a claim that biology alone confers citizenship.

The history of citizenship legislation reinforces that objection. Earlier rules subordinated mothers' independent citizenship, while later rules privileged maternity for children born out of wedlock. That change undermines an appeal to a timeless mother-child bond as sufficient justification. An apparent preference for women can enforce expectations of obligatory maternal care and absent paternal responsibility. The history supports functional scrutiny; it creates no conclusive presumption of invalid historical purpose and decides no unpresented condition.

They would remove the unconstitutional age restriction from Miller's available former-law route and direct declaratory recognition, retaining legitimation and the independent transmission prerequisites already accepted. Mathews requires attention to both equality remedies; Westcott, the benefit-conferring structure and the INA's general severability provision favor correcting the unequal barrier over withdrawing a separate maternal protection. Section 1421(d), in their view, does not bar recognizing citizenship conferred by the remaining statute after constitutional correction. That differs from equitable naturalization. They would permit ordinary implementation of the available election if needed, without a new support promise, invented election formality or hearing to relitigate accepted predicates. Their remedy imports neither the maternal one-year presence period nor an unpresented passport-processing order, and it does not declare every other §1409 condition invalid.

### Stone-Zsela's dissent

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela reaches Miller's own equality claim. He applies intermediate scrutiny to the sex classification and equivalent elevated review to the parentage rule. Government may require reliable biological proof and a timely voluntary legal parent-child relationship, but must make equivalent objective procedures available to fathers and mothers. Biological maternity may often be documented at birth; that does not justify a broader regime presuming maternal commitment and paternal absence. Records, acknowledgment, adjudication and support evidence can address legitimate proof and connection interests without that categorical asymmetry. The father's acknowledgment makes the distinction consequential here.

He would reverse and remand for a lawful equality remedy. The lower court could apply an equal acknowledgment and proof regime, allow Congress a reasonable opportunity to enact one, or recognize citizenship if no narrower lawful cure is available and the statutory prerequisites apart from the discrimination are met. His proposed remedy does not direct immediate recognition or reopen the accepted predicates. Neutral proof deadlines, safeguards against fraud and genuine legal relationships remain permissible. He defines no citizenship rule for every foreign birth and does not join the three-Justice dissent's directed former-route remedy.

#### Chaudhuri v. Tennessee; Sixth Circuit No. 96-5538; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.

[Record](../records/chaudhuri_v_tennessee_merits_1998-04-27.md#public-projection)

**Scalia, joined by Kennedy and Thomas in Part I, and by Thomas in Part II, dissenting in part.** These Justices accept the actual silence holding but would also uphold the former prayers. Part I preserves their Tanford view that a voluntary adult university ceremony is a permissible ceremonial relationship under the updated Lemon inquiry, informed by Marsh’s accommodation of ceremonial prayer. They acknowledge official attribution but reject treating this adult setting as prohibited worship merely on that basis. Part II emphasizes historical ceremonial accommodation and requires governmental compulsion to engage in religious observance, rather than official presentation of prayer alone. The University’s nonmonitoring and no-penalty account, supported by the dean’s affidavit concerning evaluations, does not establish required religious participation or penalized nonattendance. On that record Scalia and Thomas find no compulsion under their account. Kennedy does not join that methodology; he retains the distinct practical-pressure inquiry. Neither part supplies a rule binding lower courts contrary to the Court’s holding.

**Kennedy, separately dissenting in part.** Kennedy joins the adult-ceremony ground but retains Lee’s practical-pressure inquiry. Formal penalties are not indispensable to religious coercion. Here the uncontradicted nonmonitoring and no-penalty account, together with the dean’s affidavit concerning Chaudhuri’s evaluations, fails to establish the alleged practical pressure. He would affirm the former-prayer judgment on that record while leaving a materially different employment-pressure case open.

**Stevens, joined by Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, dissenting.** These Justices would affirm the circuit’s exceptional correction of its own first-application process. But the supported clerk-transition failure, actual effort to obtain consideration and independent June recall initiative establish a concrete institutional basis beyond regret about a merits result. On that ground the dissent would not impose Schlup or Sawyer as a prerequisite to recall. It makes no finding that Thompson satisfies either gateway, proves Strickland prejudice or is entitled to every merits proposition stated below.

Affirmance would preserve the direction to enter the partial rape-related writ unless California elected to retry within a reasonable time, the associated death-sentence vacation, further review of murder and the then-entered execution-order vacatur. It would not create a fixed election or trial deadline, unconditional release, a murder acquittal or an independent Supreme Court ineffective-assistance holding.

#### Ricci v. Village of Arlington Heights; No. 97-501.

[Record](../records/ricci_v_village_of_arlington_heights_merits_1998-05-04.md#public-projection)

**Ginsburg, joined by the other members of the four-Justice Part II coalition, on the unresolved application.** Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer conclude that the categorical premise foreclosed the required assessment of added restraint even though the lower court discussed continuing operation, possible daily fines, processing and duration. They would evaluate those existing facts under the actual-enforcement rule rather than decide now that custody was unlawful. A favorable judgment for defendants remains legally possible after that inquiry. No new hearing is required simply because further facts might exist, and practical processing may suffice when reasonably connected to enforcement. Wilson and Soldal permit correction of a legal framework and adverse summary judgment without a present violation finding.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in Part I and in the judgment.** Probable cause identifies the licensing violation but does not answer whether taking this identified operator from his business served a sufficient enforcement purpose. The record identifies an immediately obtainable license and a fine-only regulatory obligation, without failure to identify himself, flight, danger or another reason for removal. Stone-Zsela finds the automatic policy’s custody objectively disconnected from securing compliance or appearance and would decide it unreasonable on this record. His ground is not hidden official hostility toward the fundraising business, which Whren does not make decisive. He would remand only for municipal policy causation, preserved defenses and relief. Individual immunity must use the legal notice available in 1994; this present clarification does not retroactively defeat it. He neither creates a rule for every minor offense nor revives the settled search or abandoned probable-cause claim, and he does not join leaving the constitutional application open.

**Thomas, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Souter, dissenting.** These Justices reject unlimited authority from local permission and probable cause but find the necessary enforcement connection established here. Ricci admitted an actual continuing violation; custody lasted about an hour while officers prepared the arrest sheet, local-ordinance complaint and bond receipt and arranged recognizance release. Those tasks concerned enforcement of the same offense, unlike an unrelated additional intrusion under Ayeni. Neither the civil label nor the availability of a possible on-site citation requires proof that citation was impossible before ordinary processing. Whren, Wilson and Robinette preserve review of atypical force, unjustified duration, unrelated later detention or a method lacking a reasonable enforcement relationship. None of those broader permissions is asserted as a categorical rule here. They would affirm this actual application without deciding individual immunity.

### 1998-05-11 — Bronx Household of Faith v. Community School District No. 10; Second Circuit No. 96-9633, 127 F.3d 207. No separate Supreme Court docket supplied.

[Authoritative Public Projection](../records/bronx_household_of_faith_v_community_school_district_no_10_merits_1998-05-11.md#public-projection).

Stevens, joined by Souter and Ginsburg, agrees that the instruction exclusion impermissibly disadvantages a religious perspective on admitted subjects. He disagrees with the worship holding: an integrated recurring church service, expressly including communion, is a genuinely distinct activity rather than merely instruction from a religious perspective. Perry Education and Cornelius permit limiting the forum to the instructional, civic, social and recreational uses actually opened. Consistent exclusion is relevant to identifying that forum, although it is not sufficient by itself to establish constitutionality. The partial dissent would affirm the worship exclusion while reversing instruction. It does not claim that establishment requires exclusion or that incidental prayer in an admitted program may automatically be banned. Stone-Zsela joins this worship-activity reasoning only.

Stone-Zsela would affirm the entire judgment narrowly and order no remand. The application sought regular Sunday worship, and the stipulated record supplies no separate request for permitted discussion or instruction; he therefore treats the agreed religious-instruction rule as a limit on affirmance, not a separate judgment. He finds no comparable worship activity in the actual one-year use record and accepts a reasonable, viewpoint-neutral activity boundary. If comparable activity were established, he would reverse. His affirmance rejects the identification-with-a-church rationale and does not approve excluding a religious perspective on an admitted subject. Under Agostini, school location and religious identity do not establish governmental worship; actual official adoption could change that answer. Neither his forum position nor the Court's ruling creates a right to every building, a duty to keep the forum open or public financing of devotion.

The State has created a platform for candidates' competing private political speech, and sufficiently definite, reviewable selection standards are necessary to constrain its discretion. Cornelius's access principles, Shuttlesworth's objection to uncontrolled permit discretion and Rosenberger's neutral-allocation requirement inform that conclusion. ### 1998-05-18 — Bousley v. United States, No. 96-8516.

[Authoritative Public Projection](../records/bousley_v_united_states_merits_1998-05-18.md#public-projection).

Stevens joins the substantive and constitutional principles in Part I but would vacate the firearm conviction and permit Bousley to plead anew. Timmreck and Hill distinguish formal plea-taking defects from a constitutionally invalid plea. In his view, the erroneous understanding of the statutory element establishes the constitutional defect here, and failure to appeal does not require Bousley to prove innocence before obtaining correction. The Government would retain its ordinary burden if prosecution proceeds. His position does not require acquittal or dismissal with prejudice and does not affect the drug conviction.

Scalia, joined by Thomas, would affirm. He agrees that no cause excuses the default but rejects extending Schlup's trial-conviction gateway to guilty pleas. A plea leaves no comparable trial record of facts that participants may then have thought immaterial, may exchange admission for relief from greater charges, and may leave stale evidence insufficient to reconstruct either side of that exchange. Those features make the proposed exception materially different from Schlup's setting. The dissent does not treat possession as active use, find actual carrying, or decide Bousley's innocence.

### 1998-05-18 — Montana v. Crow Tribe of Indians, No. 96-1829.

[Authoritative Public Projection](../records/montana_v_crow_tribe_of_indians_merits_1998-05-18.md#public-projection).

Souter, joined by O'Connor, agrees that the whole-collection award cannot stand because Montana could impose a tax below the excessive level. He emphasizes that the existing request for illegally collected money encompasses a lesser claim to excessive receipts, grounded in the Tribe's own protected property interest. Interior's legally erroneous refusal and the agreement with Westmoreland do not dispose of that independent claim against the State. A dollar-for-dollar compensatory-loss measure is not the only possible basis for restitution of an improperly obtained benefit.

He would require genuine consideration of that existing claim: determine the excessive share, consider registry distributions and the remaining equities, and decide whether all, some or none of that share should be restored. This does not permit treating every state tax dollar as excessive or establish entitlement to an additional penny. The concurrence joins the Court's bounded opinion because it leaves that inquiry substantively open; its affirmative restitution framework goes beyond the Court's common holding.

### 1998-05-18 — Stewart v. Martinez-Villareal; No. 97-300.

[Authoritative Public Projection](../records/stewart_v_martinez_villareal_threshold_1998-05-18.md#public-projection).

**Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, dissenting in part.** They agree that the Court may review the circuit's threshold classification, but would reverse it. Section 2244(b)(1) addresses a claim presented in a second or successive application and requires dismissal when that claim appeared in the earlier application. Here the earlier merits application ended after other claims received merits adjudication; the Ford claim was dismissed, not retained in an ongoing proceeding. A wholly unexhausted application dismissed without prejudice presents a different situation.

For the dissenters, the court's reservation cannot create an exception that the enacted text does not supply, and the State's earlier prematurity request does not waive the statutory restriction. Ex parte Bollman's requirement of written legal authority reinforces their objection to restoring prior judicial practice after Congress changed the governing law. They would require dismissal of this repeated claim under §2244(b)(1), not an opportunity for discretionary authorization under an invented exception. They decide no competency question, order no execution and express no disposition of a genuinely separate lawful proceeding.

#### 1998-05-26 — Air Line Pilots Association v. Miller, No. 97-428.

[Public Projection](../records/air_line_pilots_association_v_miller_merits_1998-05-26.md#public-projection)

Souter delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg. Breyer dissents, joined by Stevens.

Breyer, joined by Stevens, would reverse the categorical rejection of exhaustion and remand for a bounded initial-recourse rule. Hudson's balance between prompt protection of objectors and the legitimate collection of representative expenses, informed by Street, Allen and Abood, permits an impartial, expeditious and adequate nonbinding procedure to narrow the dispute before court litigation. Their rule does not depend on contractual assent: escrow and genuinely independent judicial adjudication would protect the employees while preliminary arbitration could avoid duplicate expense. It gives the award neither preclusion nor contractual finality. Pilots who already completed arbitration have taken that step; no automatic loss follows for nonparticipants without considering the lawfulness and actual adequacy of the procedure and their posture. Both agree that a discretionary judicial pause for prompt arbitration can address practical duplication.

#### 1998-05-26 — Calderon v. Ashmus, No. 97-391.

[Public Projection](../records/calderon_v_ashmus_threshold_1998-05-26.md#public-projection)

Stone-Zsela delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Breyer concurs, joined by Souter; both also join the Court's opinion in full.

Breyer, joined by Souter, emphasizes a possible route to prompt determination in actual habeas litigation. A timely petition may present an amendment question for which chapter 154's applicability matters; the ordinary amendment rules and the more restrictive chapter-154 rules remain distinct. An appropriate ruling may also permit an interlocutory appeal under §1292(b), but only if the district court states in writing that there is a controlling legal question, substantial ground for difference of opinion and a prospect of materially advancing the litigation's termination, and the court of appeals permits an application made within ten days. An application does not itself stay proceedings. These possibilities promise no amendment, certification, appeal, exhaustion determination or additional filing time for any prisoner. They explain a concrete adjudicative route without treating convenience or aggregate efficiency as Article III jurisdiction.

#### 1998-05-26 — County of Sacramento v. Lewis, No. 96-1337.

[Public Projection](../records/county_of_sacramento_v_lewis_merits_1998-05-26.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Kennedy | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Supports reversal | Complete rapid-pursuit culpability rule, application, qualifications and remedy |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Stevens | No other Justice | Supports reversal | Individual immunity because May 22, 1990 law did not make this conduct's federal unlawfulness sufficiently apparent; reserves constitutional merits |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Scalia | Thomas | Supports reversal | Distinct constitutional ground; no join in the Court's conscience-based purpose-to-harm standard |
| Concurrence | Breyer | No other Justice | Fully joins the Court and supports reversal | Preserves flexibility to decide an appropriate case on immunity before difficult constitutional merits |

Stevens concurs only in the judgment. He would resolve the individual claim on qualified immunity without deciding the difficult constitutional standard. All relevant law existing on May 22, 1990 must be considered under the particularized-notice approach. Garner and Brower concern intentional force or intentionally applied stopping means; Checki concerns intentional misuse of police power to terrorize; Wood II concerns affirmative interference with protective circumstances. The reported pursuit decisions did not establish this claim's constitutional boundary merely by recognizing a possible egregious case, and Daniels reserved intermediate culpability. Neither the absence of an identical case nor a tally of judicial disagreement decides immunity. On the complete favorable account, the existing law did not make this pursuit's federal unlawfulness sufficiently apparent. Later decisions cannot supply retrospective notice. He makes no finding that the conduct was constitutional.

Scalia, joined by Thomas, concurs in the judgment on a different constitutional ground. The carefully described asserted right against this reckless pursuit and unintended collision lacks sufficient textual, historical or precedential support. A general protection of life or bodily security does not by itself define the constitutional tort. They reject the Court's reliance on an open-ended conscience standard and do not join its affirmative purpose-to-harm definition, although they agree that these facts establish no constitutional violation. Glucksberg does not impose a universally exclusive history method; their objection rests on the absence of adequate support for this particular asserted right and on the limits of judicially defined constitutional tort liability. Their position does not categorically exclude direct intentional assaults outside custody.

Breyer fully joins the Court. He separately preserves flexibility to decide a suitable case on qualified immunity before resolving a difficult or poorly presented constitutional question. That approach is consistent with Uhlrig and the distinction between actual wrongdoing and conduct-time notice. Today's choice to resolve the pursuit standard is not a compulsory merits-first sequence for every later case.

#### 1998-05-26 — Kiowa Tribe of Oklahoma v. Manufacturing Technologies, Inc., No. 96-1037.

[Public Projection](../records/kiowa_tribe_v_manufacturing_technologies_merits_1998-05-26.md#public-projection)

Breyer delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter. Stevens dissents, joined in full by Thomas and Ginsburg. All six members of the Court's opinion adopt the complete contract-immunity rule, its application, qualifications and dismissal mandate.

Stevens, joined by Thomas and Ginsburg, would decline to extend tribal immunity to genuinely off-reservation commercial conduct unrelated to tribal land or sovereign functions. Potawatomi resolved a trust-land operation, and Puyallup protected the tribal defendant in its own setting; neither requires the broader extension. Mescalero's ordinary-state-law baseline informs, but does not itself decide, the distinct amenability question. The dissent regards the extension as new federal common-law displacement of state adjudicatory authority without an identified federal interest sufficient to justify it. Congress's power to legislate does not compel courts to enlarge the received doctrine meanwhile, and unusually broad immunity for outside commerce burdens parties dealing beyond tribal territory.

The dissent preserves established immunity within its received scope and infers no waiver from commerce or a promise to pay. It would remand for application of its limited rule to the actual transaction and valid existing findings. The note's Carnegie recital and the creditor's Oklahoma City account remain distinct; if existing findings settle the legally material location and commercial predicates, no new factfinding is needed. Only a genuinely unresolved material predicate would require further ordinary proceedings. The dissent does not convert the location dispute into a finding against the Tribe or direct an unconditional money judgment.

#### 1998-05-26 — New Jersey v. New York, No. 120, Original.

[Public Projection](../records/new_jersey_v_new_york_original_merits_1998-05-26.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Souter | O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer throughout | Supports all six exception dispositions and recommittal | I: Compact; II: prescription; III: laches; IV: shore; V: pier; VI: convenience and decree preparation |
| Same opinion, partial join | Souter | Stone-Zsela | Supports every disposition | Parts I, II and VI; disposition only on III, IV and V, without their additional grounds |
| Same opinion, partial join | Souter | Stevens | Supports original Compact entitlement but opposes the final territorial result | Part I only |
| Concurrence | Breyer | Ginsburg | Fully joins the Court | Relevant Compact ambiguity and the significance of federal control for notice and acquiescence |
| Concurrence in Part I and dissent | Stevens | No other Justice | Would recognize New York's whole-island entitlement | Prescription proved by the cumulative sovereign practice |
| Dissent | Scalia | Thomas | Would recognize New York's whole-island entitlement | Integrated Compact interpretation through practical construction; prescription unnecessary |

The five full joiners supply a direct majority for every part. Part I additionally has Stone-Zsela and Stevens; Parts II and VI additionally have Stone-Zsela. Judgment agreement on Parts III–V adds no rationale join.

Breyer, joined by Ginsburg, fully joins the Court. They find no relevant ambiguity in Articles First and Second that displaces the background artificial-change rule, without declaring every Compact clause unambiguous or denying all contextual interpretation of silence. Federal control also matters to acquiescence. Modest civil acts may be all that a State can perform on a federally administered installation, but that does not make them adequate notice of an adverse claim or require the neighboring State to mount a major protest against each one. The contrary inference would make loss of sovereignty too easy. Conflicting federal understandings, including the Wyzanski statement and later reversals, are evidence to evaluate, not correct legal holdings that the island lies outside every State.

Stevens agrees with Part I's original Compact allocation but would find New York acquired the enlarged island by prescription. The identified fill-resident electoral and hospital records, civil administration, census treatment and public affiliation cumulatively show a continuing sovereign understanding appropriate to a federal installation. Sparse surviving examples need not negate consistent practice. He infers notice from the public character and significance of those acts and treats contrary episodes as isolated, property-related, attributable to different actors or abandoned. He does not equate every registration with an actual vote, locate every marriage on the fill or treat every federal wage choice as compulsory state law. A late protest cannot undo an acquisition already complete. The difficulties of dividing buildings reinforce his evidentiary criticism but supply no independent power to exchange territory. His sufficient prescription ground would eliminate the need for a divided-island decree.

Scalia, joined by Thomas, would recognize New York's whole-island entitlement through practical construction of the Compact, without deciding that prescription has been proved. Articles First through Third form an integrated settlement; the retained island's scope is sufficiently ambiguous for the parties' administration to inform its meaning. Article Third helps interpret the agreement even though New York advances no preserved independent claim of title under that article. Air France v. Saks, Choctaw Nation and Vermont support consulting practical construction where the agreement is ambiguous. The long treatment of the enlarged island as one New York jurisdiction, without comparable New Jersey island administration, supports their construction. Interpreting an ambiguous reservation differs from dispossessing an otherwise undoubted owner by prescription. They do not read Article Second as a transfer clause for every conceivable future fill and do not authorize exchanging a boundary once its meaning is settled. Their ground makes prescription, laches and divided-island implementation unnecessary to their preferred judgment.

#### 1998-05-27 — Waste Management, Inc. of Tennessee v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County; Sixth Circuit Nos. 95-5863 and 95-5900, 130 F.3d 731; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.

[Public Projection](../records/waste_management_v_nashville_merits_1998-05-27.md#public-projection)

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion announcing the judgment; plurality rationale | Breyer | O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg | Supports vacatur and remand of both components | Full actual-service comparison, conditional scrutiny and independent fee analysis; four rationale votes |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Joins both vacaturs and the complete remand mandate | No join in the plurality rationale; favors outright reversal on public-system and cost-bound fee grounds |
| Dissent | Kennedy | Stevens | Would affirm both reviewed determinations | Discrimination in compelled private transactions and failure of the separate fee defense |
| Dissent | Thomas | Scalia | Would reverse both determinations and end the reviewed Commerce grounds | Constitutional objection to the judicial negative Commerce Clause; no join in the renewed-Commerce mandate |

The plurality and Kennedy's dissent supply six direct supporters for the two limited purchasing and compensation propositions below. That agreement creates no additional opinion join or vote for the remand judgment.

**Breyer, joined by O'Connor, Souter and Ginsburg, announcing the judgment.** The plurality regards the lower court's categorical treatment of actual public ownership as immaterial under Carbone as an error. Carbone and SSC reserved a materially different genuine public system; neither establishes that a public plant buys every independently compelled transaction. Metro's ownership, environmental responsibility and fuel arrangement warrant comparison of the actual offering. Tracy supplies a functional inquiry tied to supported obligations; utility-style regulation is not universally indispensable, but public identity alone is insufficient. Camps prevents treating the challenged preference as its own justification.

For each measure, if a supported material public-service difference makes the measure genuinely evenhanded, Pike asks whether the interstate burden is clearly excessive relative to local benefits. If the distinction fails and discrimination is established, Metro must show a legitimate local purpose that reasonable nondiscriminatory alternatives cannot adequately serve. This does not demand perfect proof or elimination of every imaginable alternative. Competitive prices, increased municipal collection or contracts, and the reported generator/container tax remain relevant alternatives, without assumed costlessness, immediacy or equal profitability.

The fee must be examined independently. A routing distinction supplies neither an equivalent intrastate burden nor a matched compensatory charge. Its existing compensation defense fails without the identified actual burden, rough nonexcessive match and substantially equivalent taxable events required by Oregon Waste and Fulton. Another supported classification must fit the enacted incidence and actual record. Reliable disposal, fuel supply and the State's 25-percent reduction requirement are real objectives, but neither those objectives nor the absence of compensation proof establishes the ultimate validity of both measures. The remand presumes no public-service predicate, directs no automatic new hearing and guarantees no result.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in the judgment.** The Chief Justice joins vacatur and renewed adjudication of both Commerce Clause claims. He would reverse outright because directing locally generated waste to an actual public facility does not facially discriminate merely by excluding local and out-of-state private alternatives alike. In his view, Carbone's coercive favoritism toward a private enterprise leaves room for traditional municipal provision of a genuinely public disposal system. Public ownership cannot disguise private favoritism.

He would permit a diversion charge only when its incidence is nondiscriminatory and its amount genuinely corresponds to costs imposed by diverted waste. Protectionist or origin-based charges remain invalid. That qualification is not a finding of an identified equivalent intrastate tax, proved cost correspondence or a permissible amount here. His separate preference does not change the mandate he joins: neither measure is adjudged valid or invalid, and each returns for renewed classification and scrutiny. He expresses no view on the excluded takings questions.

**Kennedy, joined by Stevens, dissenting.** The dissent would affirm both determinations. Actual public ownership does not convert generators' and haulers' independent purchases into government purchases. Carbone protects competition in those compelled transactions; SSC's protection extends to performance the government actually buys. The dissent confronts the reserved public-system category but finds no supported difference in this offering sufficient to remove the compulsory transactions from discrimination scrutiny. Tracy and Camps do not make public title or stated fuel and environmental purposes decisive.

Once discrimination is found, the reported alternatives defeat the claimed necessity of these mechanisms under the legitimate-purpose and adequate-nondiscriminatory-alternatives rule. The dissent does not assume that every substitute is free, immediate or equally profitable. The fee separately lacks the identified equivalent intrastate burden required by Oregon Waste and Fulton. Affirmance would preserve lawful licensing, actual public purchases and unreviewed claims; it would prescribe no replacement tax, collection program or monetary relief.

**Thomas, joined by Scalia, dissenting.** The dissent would reverse and terminate both reviewed Commerce Clause grounds. As in their Camps constitutional position, the affirmative grant of congressional commerce power does not, in their view, authorize courts to impose this negative restriction in the absence of governing congressional legislation. They question the inference of exclusivity from that grant, the conversion of congressional silence into a prohibition, and judicial policy balancing. They expressly seek displacement of contrary precedent; they do not contend it has already been overruled.

Their comparative observations under existing precedent do not supply assent to renewed service classification, discrimination justification or Pike balancing. Ordinary mandate proceedings on independently preserved matters may continue, but these Commerce claims would end. Ginsburg's narrower comparison position does not join this constitutional repudiation. Thomas's tentative Import-Export alternative in Camps supplies no disposition of these routing and per-ton measures: no preserved presentation, established import/export status or definitive applicable rule is supplied here.

O'Connor delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine adopt the narrow restraint, arbitrary-selection and conduct-time immunity holdings with their individual-proof limits. Scalia files a concurrence, joined by Thomas, preserving their direct-restraint basis and rejecting any implication that they adopt a broader conscience framework. Their concurrence withholds assent from no proposition actually adopted by the Court.

Scalia, joined by Thomas, concurs fully in the narrow opinion. DeShaney's direct-restraint principle and Collins's distinction between voluntary exposure and compulsion support this alleged affirmative deprivation. They do not adopt a free-standing judicial-shock inquiry or a general duty to rescue persons from private danger. Lewis's distinct reckless-pursuit claim therefore does not compel the same merits result here. Thomas's disagreement with Farmer's Eighth Amendment punishment predicate remains; today's direct-deprivation holding neither converts that judgment concurrence into a full Farmer join nor transplants every prison rule to roadside custody.

They also join the narrow equality and immunity holdings. Moreno's bare-harm prohibition, preserved in their Romer position, does not depend on a suspect classification. Bowers does not license deliberate hostile selection under unrelated traffic laws. Actual comparison, purpose, effect, personal conduct and the old prohibition must do the work. Their concurrence supports no broader framework than the Court adopts and no finding that the disputed allegations have been proved.

Stevens would preserve the conditional habeas relief. #### Muscarello v. United States, No. 96-1654; Cleveland et al. v. United States, No. 96-8837. — 1998-06-08

[Controlling Record](../records/muscarello_cleveland_v_united_states_merits_1998-06-08.md#public-projection).

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas | Affirmance in both dockets | Entire opinion |
| Dissent | Ginsburg | Scalia, Souter | Would reverse and remand both dockets | Contextual armed-carriage construction and residual lenity |

Ginsburg, joined by Scalia and Souter, would reverse and remand both cases. In the use-or-carry context, they read carrying a firearm as bearing an arm on or about the person, including sufficiently close carriage approximating a holster or pocket. Literal bodily contact is unnecessary, and carrying an accessible weapon remains distinct from actively using it. Generic examples of transporting objects do not eliminate the narrower meaning of the particular firearm phrase.

At minimum, the competing established usages leave genuine uncertainty after interpretation. Ratzlaf's residual-lenity rule therefore bars imposing the additional five-year term on the broader transportation construction. The trafficking-relation element cannot resolve ambiguity about what conduct counts as carrying. Other firearm provisions and ordinary sentencing consequences also undermine any need to stretch this particular enhancement to avoid a supposed punishment gap; that observation creates no universal sentencing rule. The dissent would not order acquittal or foreclose an independently available ground outside the reviewed question.

#### National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt; D.C. Circuit No. 96-5354 — 1998-06-08

[Controlling Record](../records/national_association_of_home_builders_v_babbitt_merits_1998-06-08.md#public-projection).

Souter delivers the Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer. Stone-Zsela files a concurrence, joined by no other Justice, while joining the complete Court opinion and judgment. O'Connor files a dissent, joined in full by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring.** The Chief Justice joins the Court's economic-conversion ground and affirmance. He also states his preferred framework for noneconomic intrastate conduct: inclusion reasonably necessary to prevent evasion or material impairment of a valid interstate regime, or a materially supported substantial interstate externality that individual States cannot reasonably confine or internalize. Hale establishes the first route; the second is his proposed development of Lopez and is not adopted by the Court.

For the proposed externality route, the Government must identify the regulated class, the concrete cross-border ecological, commercial or comparable effect, its substantial rather than speculative character, the affected States' inability reasonably to internalize or control it through ordinary territorial authority, and a reasonable fit between the prohibition and that spillover. Courts independently decide constitutional eligibility; Congress receives substantial latitude on predictive and empirical judgments once the mechanism is identified. The Government must point to a materially adequate legislative or adjudicative basis, and courts may not invent a market, causal pathway, externality or anti-evasion necessity.

National importance, biodiversity, tourism, research, development pressure, possible future value and similar problems occurring in several States do not alone establish either route. He proposes no fixed number of States, incidents, dollars or species, market percentage, scientific threshold, universal formal-findings requirement, clear-and-convincing burden or defendant-specific congressional findings. Actual interstate sale, transport, trafficking, migratory movement or another independently sufficient mechanism remains distinct. He does not make every ecosystem national or every species a commodity.

On that preferred analysis, the lower judgments do not adequately determine a supported externality or impairment of an identified interstate regime, and further mechanism inquiry would ordinarily be needed. His operative vote nevertheless joins the Court's sufficient economic-activity ground and leaves the judgment standing without remand. His additional framework and evidence inquiry are noncontrolling.

**O'Connor, dissenting, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.** The dissent would reverse and remand for relief confined to the reviewed applications. Lopez requires a connection fitted to the class Congress enacted. Section 9 prohibits taking listed wildlife, including habitat-caused injury, without defining that class by economic exchange. The projects' construction activity is real, but selecting its economic attributes does not for the dissent supply the missing fit. Hinds likewise refuses to substitute an owner's purchases for the statute's actual predicate. American Life League, Robinson and Bird involved prohibitions operating directly on service markets or commercial assets; that relationship cannot simply be transferred to all injury to a species.

The dissent accepts that Congress may regulate genuine economic land conversion for environmental ends under Hodel and include intrastate conduct through Hale's demonstrated anti-evasion relationship. It finds neither sufficient enacted-class fit nor an alternative supported regime mechanism here. Comprehensive conservation, potential medical value and generalized biodiversity benefits cannot replace that showing. The dissent obeys Sweet Home's statutory construction and causal limits, creates no categorical immunity for intrastate wildlife or traditional state subjects, and would invalidate neither the entire ESA nor all habitat regulation. Its confined relief would grant no blanket development permit and decide no actual taking or permit entitlement.

**Justice Souter, concurring.** He joins the Court's opinion and its distinction between knowing unlawful dealing and knowing the licensing requirement. He emphasizes that the later no-lawbreaking instruction is erroneous: had that specific objection been raised and preserved, he would vacate. Those conditions are not present in the reported appellate posture, so the reservation supplies no relief here and is not a judgment-only join.

**Justice Scalia, dissenting, joined by Justice Ginsburg.** They would require awareness that dealing without the required license is forbidden, without requiring the defendant to identify the Code section or federal source by name. Congress made the object of willfulness a violation of the licensing provision; knowing some collateral aspect of the transaction is illegal does not establish knowing violation of that duty. Ratzlaf's treatment of a known reporting duty and a separate structuring prohibition supports identifying the actual charged prohibition, and Staples rejects replacing the offense's fault with dangerousness. At minimum, unresolved contextual ambiguity calls for lenity. They would reverse and remand for count-specific application of that rule and the preserved sufficiency contention. Actual evidentiary insufficiency would require the ordinary acquittal consequence, not a new trial to repair deficient proof; they order no automatic acquittal of every conspiracy or substantive count and calculate no new sentence.

### Hohn v. United States; No. 96-8986. — 1998-06-15

[Controlling Record](../records/hohn_v_united_states_threshold_1998-06-15.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|

#### Separate Writings

**Justice Scalia, dissenting, with Justice Thomas throughout and Justice O’Connor in Part I.** Part I would preserve House’s statutory construction. Section 2253 conditions the taking of an appeal on a certificate; until a circuit justice or judge gives that permission, the underlying case has not entered the court of appeals in the sense §1254 requires. The decision of a judge on permission is not a separate appellate case merely because the request involves legal judgment. Congress retained and extended the certificate structure against House’s settled construction, strengthening the statutory-stare-decisis objection. Felker’s express bar concerns permission for initial district consideration of a successive application, a different act for which House supplied no controlling construction; Stewart concerns a different circuit classification. Neither warrants discarding the certificate-specific precedent.

Part II, joined only by Thomas, rejects the no-certificate alternative because the provision regulates the appellate step initiated after AEDPA’s enactment. Applying it to the July 29, 1996 notice is prospective at the relevant activity; it does not impose a new merits rule on the earlier district motion. They make no forfeiture finding. Without statutory review authority they would dismiss, not vacate the denial. They grant no extraordinary writ and do not treat §1651 as an independent source of jurisdiction.

**Justice O’Connor, separately dissenting.** She joins the House and statutory-jurisdiction analysis in Part I but states a narrower temporal ground. Landgraf requires attention first to statutory direction and the particular provision, not a generic procedural label. Lindh’s application-date construction for the amendments governing the pending district application does not settle the separate appellate condition. Section 2253(c) regulates the later appeal initiated on July 29, 1996; applying it there is consistent with Felker’s separately examined post-enactment authorization and review proceedings. She therefore rejects Hohn’s alternative on that provision-specific basis, without resolving every chapter-153 amendment or finding his argument forfeited. She would dismiss for want of statutory jurisdiction.

### Phillips v. Washington Legal Foundation; No. 96-1578. — 1998-06-15

[Controlling Record](../records/phillips_v_washington_legal_foundation_merits_1998-06-15.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas | Complete ownership rule, its qualifications and affirmance; later constitutional consequences remain reserved. |
| Dissent | Souter | Stevens, Ginsburg, Breyer | Would vacate for integrated consideration of property, taking and compensation; also joins Breyer’s alternative answer if ownership is reached alone. |
| Separate dissent | Breyer | Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg | Joins the integrated-remand disposition and supplies the alternative objection to client ownership of the otherwise unavailable return. |

#### Separate Writings

**Justice Souter, dissenting, joined by Justices Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer.** The dissent would vacate the limited judgment and remand for the lower courts to consider property, taking and compensation together. The legal and economic arrangement matters to whether an isolated title declaration has any consequence under the Takings Clause. Roth’s reference to existing entitlements does not require examining one incident of ownership apart from the rules making that interest available. Penn Central directs attention to economic impact, reasonable investment-backed expectations and the character of governmental action, while compensation ordinarily concerns the owner’s loss rather than the recipient’s gain. Those matters could defeat a takings claim, but the dissent would have the lower courts decide them rather than declare no taking or zero compensation here.

The dissent accepts that property identification and valuation are distinct, but regards their isolated treatment in this case as liable to distort the full constitutional inquiry. It does not approve confiscation of the principal, which unquestionably belongs to the client. A claim concerning compulsory use of that principal remains available for lawful consideration even under the dissenters’ alternative rejection of the asserted interest entitlement. The four also join Breyer’s alternative analysis if the Court decides ownership alone.

**Justice Breyer, separately dissenting, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg.** He joins Souter’s proposed integrated remand. If ownership is reached in isolation, he would reject the claimed entitlement for funds properly placed under the no-net-return program rule. The operative arrangement makes a charitable return possible where a client otherwise has no legally and economically realizable net benefit. Webb’s involved an independently productive fund; its protection against public relabeling does not settle ownership of this otherwise unavailable return. Lucas protects established entitlements without deciding how this claimed benefit must be identified.

This argument does not assume that every individual is legally barred from a NOW account. Individual eligibility, restrictions on corporate and partnership funds, administrative and reporting costs, and the distinction between gross and net yield must remain separate. The Federal Reserve interpretation is part of the banking setting, not a holding that its validity has been adjudicated. The reported Texas concession allows assessment of net client earnings through feasible attorney pooling; it establishes no positive alternative yield for these particular funds. Funds capable of earning net client interest belong outside IOLTA, and diversion of such interest or principal presents a different question. The dissent fixes no compensation amount, accepts no public-purpose exemption from the Takings Clause and does not direct final judgment against every claim.

### Zeran v. America Online, Inc.; Fourth Circuit No. 97-1523; no separate Supreme Court docket established. — 1998-06-15

[Controlling Record](../records/zeran_v_america_online_inc_merits_1998-06-15.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Stevens | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Eight join the provision-specific temporal rule, its limits and reversal with remand. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | Stevens | O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Five join the complete Landgraf organizing explanation. |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Scalia | Kennedy, Thomas | Joins Part I; states the distinct relevant-activity basis and withholds Part II's general-framework join. |
| Dissent | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Would affirm on both temporal direction and publisher-treatment grounds. |

#### Separate Writings

**Justice Scalia, concurring in part and in the judgment, joined by Justices Kennedy and Thomas.** They join Part I's temporal holding and remand but not Part II's full organizing explanation. Their relevant-activity inquiry identifies the publication-related conduct whose legal responsibility the statute regulates. The enforcement clause cannot be detached from the substantive publisher-treatment rule and read as though filing were its only regulated event. The text gives no direction to attach the new protection to the completed conduct here. Kennedy's Hughes Aircraft opinion likewise rejects later filing as conclusive when substantive legal consequences change. They adopt no constitutional vested-claim rule and do not decide prospective distributor liability.

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, dissenting.** He would affirm the judgment on the pleadings on two necessary statutory grounds. First, the original §230(d)(3) addresses both causes brought and liability imposed after enactment. In his view, those commands supply the temporal direction Landgraf requires, and applying them to this April 23, 1996 action follows that direction despite the earlier provider conduct. Hughes Aircraft lacked comparable temporal language and therefore does not control the result.

Second, he would hold the pleaded notice-based distributor duties within §230(c)(1). Notice may change a distributor's fault standard, but duties to remove, retract, investigate or screen another person's information remain duties concerning publication. AOL did not become the information's creator or materially develop it merely by receiving notice. He would leave these notice-based claims dismissed while preserving independently enforceable promises and claims not dependent on publisher status under their own elements. His position does not protect the original author, information AOL created or materially developed, conduct outside the statutory definitions, or claims within the statute's express preservation provisions. Recordkeeping remains unresolved. Neither ground of this dissent supplies a holding of the Court.

### Caron v. United States, No. 97-6270. — 1998-06-22

[Controlling Record](../records/caron_v_united_states_merits_1998-06-22.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone-Zsela | Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer | Complete conviction-status rule, application to the actual residual restriction, reservations and affirmance. |
| Dissent | Thomas | Scalia, Souter | Would reverse and remand on the express-prohibition construction and independently on residual lenity. |

#### Separate Writings

**Justice Thomas, dissenting, joined by Justices Scalia and Souter.** The three would reverse and remand because Massachusetts did not expressly prohibit firearm possession in the sense required by the federal exception. It allowed rifles and shotguns and even allowed handguns in the home or business. A restriction on handgun possession elsewhere does not amount to the express prohibition that, on their reading, prevents restored convictions from being excluded.

Their construction also treats the conviction as the statutory unit. It does not make the same conviction exist federally for a forbidden handgun and disappear for a permitted rifle. They choose the defendant's side of the all-or-nothing inquiry: because the restoration does not contain the required complete possession prohibition, these restored convictions are excluded. Beecham's sovereign selector supports consulting the actual restoration but did not decide this partial-restriction question. Federal protective purpose cannot replace Congress's chosen express condition.

Independently, the textually natural restoration reading remains at least sufficiently unresolved after context and purpose are examined to require lenity. Chapman and Granderson reserve that principle for ambiguity surviving ordinary interpretation; the dissent relies on the actual statutory difficulty, not merely the existence of two proposed readings. It would remove this unless-clause basis for counting the Massachusetts convictions and return the reviewed sentencing consequences for lawful disposition. It orders neither acquittal on all counts nor exclusion of every other predicate, and it decides no constitutional challenge. Both the textual ground and residual-lenity ground have the assent of all three dissenters.

### Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School District, No. 96-1866. — 1998-06-22

[Controlling Record](../records/gebser_v_lago_vista_independent_school_district_merits_1998-06-22.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Stone-Zsela | Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Five directly reject actual-corrective-official notice as the exclusive attribution route, with the stated limits. |
| Opinion announcing the judgment, Parts II–III | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Part II states the narrower attribution ground with the component-specific Marks force identified in Holdings; Part III gives his own record application. The four other reversal supporters do not join these parts. |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Breyer | Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg | Joins Part I and supports reversal/remand; states independent actual-authority/material-aid and negligent-correction grounds. |
| Separate concurrence | Ginsburg | Souter, Breyer | Proposes the limited avoidable-harm defense within their broader framework; Stevens reserves it and Stone-Zsela leaves defenses unresolved. |
| Dissent | O'Connor | Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Would affirm under Kinman's exclusive actual-notice rule and its record-specific insufficiency application. |

#### Separate Writings

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's opinion announcing the judgment, Part III.** The complaint to the principal, the internal warning and the evidence about the absence of a functioning grievance route create, in his view, a factual dispute about the recipient's own fault. He would require the lower courts to examine whether school-conferred authority materially enabled the discrimination and whether actual recipient knowledge or willfully blind, deliberately indifferent reporting failure caused its continuation. A district cannot defeat that inquiry through its own failure to transmit substantial warning information. He does not treat the complaint about classroom remarks as an established report of a sexual relationship, resolve the conflicting policy evidence, or find liability. Employment, ordinary negligence and a technical regulatory violation alone remain insufficient. This record-specific application has no other joins; the attribution component of Part II has only the limited Marks force stated above.

**Justice Breyer, concurring in part and in the judgment, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg.** They join Part I's rejection of exclusivity and support reversal and ordinary remand, but do not join Parts II–III. They renew the two independent attribution routes previously stated in their Kinman position. First, actual delegated educational power materially aiding intentional harassment can attribute the wrong to the recipient without a separate higher-management knowledge requirement. Second, negligent failure to correct after responsible officials knew or reasonably should have known, causing injury or continuation, supplies an independent ground. Teacher title or opportunity alone does not establish actual aid, and a policy breach alone establishes neither negligence nor causation.

Franklin permits compensation for intentional discrimination. These Justices distinguish the teacher's intentional wrong from the agency principles attributing that wrong; their negligence alternative is not compensation for every unintended discriminatory effect. Cannon supplies the established private action, while Title IX's administrative notice and correction process does not require a second intentional wrong by recipient management in every damages case. They acknowledge that Kinman had rejected their broader grounds and would reconsider that exclusivity. Title VII's agency decisions supply a limited analogy, not an automatic transfer of every employment rule.

The actual delegation, material aid, information received, correction, reporting arrangements and causal injury require ordinary further consideration. The affidavit/deposition tension over policy and uncertainty about dissemination are evidence, not conclusive findings. These Justices do not establish liability or compel a trial. Their judgment agreement does not endorse Stone-Zsela's record-specific awareness reasoning. Their broader attribution theories do not become controlling merely because they support the same judgment; only the narrower component identified in Holding II has the stated Marks force.

**Justice Ginsburg, separately concurring, joined by Justices Souter and Breyer.** Within their broader attribution framework, these three would permit a limited avoidable-consequences defense. The district would bear the burden of proving that internal remedies were adequately publicized and likely to provide redress without undue risk, effort or expense. Recovery would be barred only to the extent the plaintiff unreasonably failed to use those measures and consequently suffered avoidable harm. A paper policy, nonreporting alone, an unsafe or ineffective route or eventual correction would not establish the defense. The uncertain policy and dissemination record does not conclusively establish it here. This is a causal limit on avoidable recovery, not automatic complete immunity or an additional Court-adopted attribution condition. Stevens reserves the defense and does not join its terms; Stone-Zsela leaves defenses unresolved.

**Justice O'Connor, dissenting, joined by Justices Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.** They would affirm under Kinman's actual-notice and deliberate-disregard rule. Franklin's availability of compensation does not answer recipient responsibility. Title IX's recipient structure, its administrative correction mechanism and Pennhurst's notice principle support attention to the recipient's own culpable nonresponse rather than ordinary agency attribution or knowledge imputed from the teacher's conduct. They would preserve Kinman's exclusivity and reject the additional attribution route.

Even assuming that the principal had corrective authority, the reported information and response do not, in their view, establish actual knowledge of the relationship or a substantial risk followed by deliberate and unreasonable disregard. The parents complained about classroom comments. The principal met with Waldrop, received an apology and assurance, cautioned him and informed the guidance counselor; termination followed police discovery. These responses are not declared perfect, and a warning does not invariably suffice. But this record does not establish the required culpable refusal to protect.

The possible absence of a functioning complaint procedure is not itself institutional actual notice. The principal's information cannot be pooled with Waldrop's knowledge, and the policy conflict cannot be resolved by assuming that every procedure was absent. Their rule requires neither a written complaint, a victim's personal report, a confession nor proof that a completed sexual relationship was already known. Actual notice of a substantial danger can suffice. Administrative and injunctive enforcement remain distinct, and the district receives no personal qualified immunity. These four oppose both reversal and the limitation of Kinman.

### Pennsylvania Board of Probation & Parole v. Scott; No. 97-581. — 1998-06-22

[Controlling Record](../records/pennsylvania_board_of_probation_parole_v_scott_merits_1998-06-22.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg, Breyer | Complete bounded institutional-deterrence rule, reservations and affirmance. |
| Concurrence | Stevens | No other Justice | Joins the Court in full and adds a distinct constitutional-remedy explanation. |
| Dissent | Kennedy | O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas | Would reverse the federal exclusion requirement and remand on the ordinary-revocation cost/deterrence ground. |

#### Separate Writings

**Justice Stevens, concurring.** He joins the Court’s institutional-deterrence ground and judgment, while also regarding a meaningful exclusionary remedy as constitutionally necessary to make the Fourth Amendment effective. His positions in Leon and Segura treat judicial use of unlawfully obtained evidence as more than a matter of administrative preference. The investigating officers and revoking authority belong to the same enforcement system; allowing that system the ordinary benefit of its unlawful search would impair the right itself. He does not decide consent, require exclusion for every collateral use or impose all criminal-trial procedure on revocation. His additional constitutional characterization is his own, not a ground adopted by the other Justices joining the Court.

**Justice Kennedy, dissenting, joined by Justices O’Connor, Scalia and Thomas.** The dissent would reverse the federal exclusion requirement and remand. A Fourth Amendment violation does not automatically determine the remedy in each later forum. Calandra and Janis require examination of additional deterrence against the costs of withholding relevant evidence. Morrissey and Gagnon recognize a supervisory process concerned with compliance during conditional liberty; exclusion would obstruct that function and require additional search litigation.

The dissent acknowledges that these searchers were parole officers who knew Scott’s status, and that their institution could benefit from revocation use. It nevertheless considers the added deterrence insufficient to justify the evidentiary and administrative costs in the ordinary revocation setting presented. It relies on no finding that parole officers never investigate crime, that this search was lawful, or that discipline and civil damages proved effective. Evans’s specific clerical-reliance exception is not transplanted. The proposed reversal would remove this federal exclusion requirement, not establish admissibility under every other rule, extinguish available state law, order a new revocation or decide exceptional abuse not established here.

### United States v. Bajakajian; No. 96-1487. — 1998-06-22

[Controlling Record](../records/united_states_v_bajakajian_merits_1998-06-22.md#public-projection).

#### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Relationship and scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Thomas | Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer throughout; Stone-Zsela in Parts I and III; O'Connor, Scalia and Kennedy in Parts I and II | I: punitive coverage, gross disproportionality and rejection of a categorical instrumentality prerequisite. II: appellate review. III: actual excessiveness and bounded affirmance. |
| Dissent in part | Kennedy | O'Connor, Scalia | All three join Parts I–II but reject Part III’s application and would permit the full statutory forfeiture. |

#### Separate Writings

**Justice Kennedy, dissenting in part, joined by Justices O’Connor and Scalia.** They join punitive coverage, the gross-disproportionality standard, independent legal review and rejection of the circuit’s instrumentality prerequisite. They disagree with the application and would reverse the refusal of full forfeiture.

The amount concealed measures the scale of a deliberate failure to report. Congress may punish that wrong seriously without establishing that the funds were criminal proceeds or proving a second offense. Reporting helps detect financial crime that otherwise may remain hidden; treating the absence of a proved additional crime as decisive undervalues that preventive function. The five-year and $250,000 statutory maxima and the expressly mandated forfeiture demonstrate substantial legislative seriousness. The $5,000 Guidelines fine operates alongside, rather than silently replacing, forfeiture.

In their view the full amount remains within the demanding constitutional boundary despite lawful source and intended use. Their ground adds no laundering or trafficking finding and does not treat dismissal of the false-statement count as a conviction. They reject neither fines coverage nor the need for an individualized constitutional judgment, and they do not reopen the conviction, probation or ordinary fine. The disagreement supplies no ruling on the unappealed $15,000 amount.
